title: The last good meal before the front
content: A warm bowl of borscht in a cold country, after a long day of work. Maybe that's what happiness is all about. I'm sitting in Trypichchia, a traditional restaurant in Kharkiv, a city about 30 km from Russian positions. And this borscht, I swear to god, might be the best I've ever had in my entire life. As a devoted enthusiast, I've eaten it in every possible setting: in fancy restaurants, at petrol stations, in village canteens, in shelters, and in trenches. I know my borscht. Mykyta, 29, one of the founders, tells us that the place started out as a local canteen at the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion. Its sole purpose was to feed soldiers and volunteers who had stayed in the city when Russian forces were on the verge of capturing it. Since then, it has grown into a 300-sq-metre restaurant dedicated to one thing: “Serving the best food at the lowest price while rediscovering Ukrainian cuisine in a Kharkiv that has been Russified for far too long.” And you can feel it. title: Here, have some cancer with your smoky bacon crisps
content: The taste of smoke triggers memories of cosy firesides and tasty barbecues. Think smoked ham, smoked salmon, smoked cheese, and the less traditional smoky bacon crisps. Smoke flavourings are usually made by burning wood, capturing the smoke, and turning it into a liquid that can be added to food. But these smoky flavours may damage DNA and risk causing cancer, EU food experts said in 2023, leading to an EU ban on eight substances that came into effect in July for flavours added to sauces, soups, and snacks. And more are now set to be snuffed out: a wider ban on smoke flavourings in ham, fish, and cheese will land in 2029. The traditional method of exposing food to smoke and heat in a smokehouse oven, though it too can introduce some toxic compounds, is still allowed. The flavourings industry has tried, and failed, to fight back. Food flavourings companies Kerry Inc and Kerry Ingredients last week lost their legal fight to overturn the ban for three flavours they make. Kerry and other manufacturers have been trying to find smoky alternatives or evoke smokiness with herbs, spices, or salt, with limited success. title: The trouble with pet turtles and pink flowers
content: If you went on a walk this summer, you might not have noticed anything out of place. Pink flowers blooming near the riverbank. A turtle with a red stripe behind its eye sunbathing on a log. A raccoon enjoying its breakfast next to your rubbish bin. But the Himalayan balsam, pond slider, and raccoon that you might have seen are all on an EU list of species it considers a major threat to native ones. The list of “invasive alien species of Union concern” currently includes 114 plant and animal species that were introduced accidentally or deliberately into a natural environment where they are not normally found. EU countries are required to try to prevent accidental introductions, catch and eradicate new arrivals quickly, and manage the species that have already become widespread. A TEC analysis of the geographical spread of 75 invasive alien species of Union concern show that 83% are present in more than one country, and 60% are reported in at least five. The success of invasive alien species can be attributed to a couple of important shared characteristics, according to Piero Genovesi, biologist and chair of the IUCN SSC Invasive Species Specialist Group. title: No olives left to pick
content: It's olive harvest time in Italy, but in many parts of Puglia, there's nothing left to pick. Since 2013, the bacterium Xylella fastidiosa has killed at least 20 million olive trees in Salento alone. The bacterium chokes the tree’s water supply until it dries out. In areas near the outbreak, every host plant within 50 metres of a new case must be felled to prevent the disease spreading. An estimated 33,000 jobs have been lost in Puglia, according to the farmers’ association Confagricoltura. “This is the most serious agronomic problem in the EU,” said Patrizio Ziggiotti, secretary general of the Puglia-based charity Save The Olives, which was set up to confront the crisis and help farmers. The bacterium is thought to have arrived on ornamental plants from Central America, and has since been detected in Spain, France, and Portugal. Olives are central to southern European history and culture. In Greek mythology, Athena won the patronage of Athens by giving the city an olive tree. title: The information war in your comments
content: “Spamouflage” is an operation you may never have heard of. It best embodies a phenomenon we likely all interact with on a daily basis on social media: coordinated state-backed attempts to manipulate online conversations. In 2023, Meta took down 7,704 Facebook accounts and 954 Pages belonging to Spamouflage, a Chinese bot network it linked to Chinese law enforcement. Hundreds of accounts posted comments on Facebook written to sound “personal” and aimed at Western governments, voters, and critics of Beijing. One bot wrote that the 6 January attack on the US Capitol “made the world see the hypocrisy and unbearable [sic] of ‘American democracy,'” according to influence operation tracker Graphika. Fake commenters often adopt invented identities. “Sometimes the bots are even given a bit of personality, like ‘I'm a Black American’ or ‘I'm a doctor in the Midwest,’” Darren Linvill, co-director of Clemson University's Media Forensics Hub, told TEC. Spamouflage accounts replying to news outlets and public figures typically criticise or harass them. Some pose as members of groups tied to those they are attacking, Graphika analyst Lili Turner told TEC. AI makes these tactics easier to deploy.

title: The electric truck is ready. Europe is not
content: Your latest online delivery probably travelled to you by road, and so does a quarter of all other goods delivered in the EU. The final stretch is usually covered by small vans, many of them electric, but heavy trucks were also likely involved in connecting manufacturers and smaller couriers. And those are still mainly powered by diesel engines. By 2030, an EU law requires heavy-duty truck and bus manufacturers to cut the carbon emissions of the vehicles they produce by 45% compared to 2019. According to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), that means at least a third of all new trucks currently bought in the EU need to be zero-emission, mainly electric. Now, fewer than 3% are. For manufacturers, shifting production to e-trucks only makes sense if there's demand. “Obviously, you don't produce these vehicles without having someone who wants to buy them,” Thomas Fabian from ACEA told The European Correspondent. And why aren't people buying? Lack of charging infrastructure, mainly. title: Rare sighting: European leaders at COP31
content: Last week, we introduced you to the creatures of COP31. Today, we zoom in on a species that seems to be slowly going extinct at the global climate conference: the European leader. Habitat: under threat. In 2025, the world saw an extreme weather event every day on average, according to the Climate Risk Index. Spain ranked third among those most affected, and France, Italy, and Romania also made the top 20. In European cities, 50,000 people are estimated to have died from heat this summer alone. Population trend: declining. Only five of the EU's 27 national leaders came to the Leaders' Summit, where heads of state and government address the conference. Austria, Slovenia, and Finland sent their presidents, who have little say over climate policy, while only Malta and Cyprus sent the person who actually runs their government. The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, did show up, though she didn't mention fossil fuels in her brief speech. title: The EU sidelines its top diplomat
content: The EU has a top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, to jet around the world meeting with global leaders on behalf of its 27 member states. She's the international face of the EU, meant to represent all EU citizens and their interests in the world. Except when she isn't. Last week, EU governments picked five countries for potential negotiations with Russia to discuss ways to end its war against Ukraine: France, Germany, Italy, Poland, and one non-EU member, the United Kingdom. These are known as the E5 group of “Europe's five leading military powers”. Also on the list: EU representatives from the European Commission and the European Council, which organises meetings of EU leaders. Wait, back up a bit, there are talks with Russia? Sort of. The United States has been holding talks between Russia and Ukraine for several months to try and end the war. They haven't made any real progress, but they have agreed to swap prisoners. The talks haven't involved European governments who provide virtually all financial support to Ukraine, until this month. Ukraine has consistently asked for Europe to be included. title: Searching for a good day for honey
content: On a perfect summer's day in Latvia, there’s barely any wind and the flowers are producing nectar. “20 degrees and up, with sunshine – that’s an ideal day,” says Valters Brusbārdis, who kept bees for 30 years before selling them all last spring. He also chairs the Latvian Beekeepers’ Association. June and July are usually the most reliable months for making honey, he said. For a professional beekeeper in Latvia, more than 50kg of honey per colony makes a good season. Some of his fellow beekeepers told him they’d had record harvests this year. In 2023, Eurostat counted a record 9.4 million hives on EU farms, 16% more than in 2020. Italy had the highest number, followed by Romania, and Greece. But the figures exclude wild bees, and tell us nothing about the health of the bees living in these hives. Bees and the climate In Bulgaria’s Pirin Mountains, beekeeper Ivan Geshev has seen the effects of the climate crisis on his bees since 2016, from droughts to sharp temperature swings. He estimates that his summer worker bees now live five or six days less than they used to, leaving fewer bees to collect pollen and nectar. title: The antidote to TikTok tourism? A free paper map
content: Planning a city trip in Europe? Chances are you’ll scroll TikTok for ideas or ask ChatGPT to build an itinerary. But have you considered using a paper map instead? Sound old-school? It might be what you actually need. Meet USE-IT Europe, a network of free city maps made by young locals who want to share with visitors where they actually spend their time. The maps cover the usual ground – where to eat, drink, shop, relax – but each one also comes with a five-minute history of the city and an “Act like a local” section full of dos and don’ts. In Prague for example, don’t order the chimney cake. It’s “not Czech, not traditional, and not so good.” Depending on the city, you might also find Spotify playlists, useful local phrases, and suggestions on what to order at a bar or bring to a picnic in the park. The maps are full of practical tips too, from free concerts to places where you can get free tap water. “Honest tourist information from locals for young travellers. title: Is this really the future we want?
content: Nine robots dance clumsily on the stage of Lisbon's FIL Arena. “This is our time, this is our fight” go the lyrics of the song. “This was the biggest robot dance performance outside of China!” the event's moderator proclaims. The 30,000 people in the arena give the robots a round of applause. The cameras filming the robots, however, are still operated by human videographers. I'm at the opening of Web Summit, one of the world's largest tech conferences, held annually in Lisbon. It draws 70,000 attendees encompassing the entire tech sector, from mega-corporations such as Meta, Apple, and Tiktok, to small start-ups, as well as countries from around the world showing off their industry. Attendees pay a lot to be there. General admission tickets cost around €1,500, unless you're a journalist, then you get in for free. I went to find out what the tech sector envisions for the future. Its biggest buzzword right now is agentic AI, which is marketed as a personal assistant for your daily life: think booking flights, working with Excel spreadsheets, or replying to that email you've left sitting in your inbox for too long. title: The grand art-taking - Tracking Europe's missing paintings
content: Over the past century, art thieves have stolen 27 Van Gogh masterpieces across Europe, more than any other famous artist by a healthy margin. But if you add up mainstream cinema hits, TV series, and even docu-dramas, the favourite victim is Rembrandt, followed by Degas and Rubens. Van Gogh’s lead owes a lot to one very ambitious night. On 14 April 1991, 20 paintings vanished from Amsterdam’s Van Gogh Museum. Two armed men had hidden inside the building and, as it turned out, had help from within. Yet the world-famous Dutch painter remains underrepresented on screen, appearing in just two action films: The Train and the less-known Righteous Thieves, both involving Nazi art plundered during World War II. As for locations, both real-life and fictional art theft love glamorous capitals like Paris and London. Where the film industry exaggerates is the method: forged copies, disguises, and acrobatic roof-suspension instead of nighttime break-ins and improvised ladders. In films, masterpieces usually end up back on the wall. In reality, some never make it home. title: Berlin's big plan to evict its landlords
content: Tobi lives in a 50 sq metre apartment in Berlin-Neukölln. His landlord, the real estate company Deutsche Wohnen, thinks it has a storage room. It does not. Every two years, Deutsche Wohnen sends Tobi a letter announcing a rent increase, listing the storage room as a feature that has not yet been priced into his rent. Each time, Tobi refuses. “I respond that no, I still don’t have a storage room. Or they tell me that my bathroom tiles, which are plain white except for two small lines of red and orange square tiles, are a value-adding feature. Some things are really silly.” In 11 years, he’s turned down five increases. In the same block, Jen has had a leak above her kitchen for three years. “I’ve reported it eight times. Sometimes you get an inspection appointment, someone comes, looks at it, and then nothing happens. title: Locked up and handed a pill
content: “Can you imagine being locked in one place from morning to night?” Federico Mollo, 51, told The European Correspondent. He spent eight years in Italian prisons between 2011 and 2019 for a homicide conviction. From prison, he completed a high school diploma, worked, took writing classes, and joined the prison's band. “I did everything I could,” he said. “Being locked in a cage makes you lose your mind.” About one third of European prisoners suffer from mental health disorders, according to a 2021 survey by the World Health Organization (WHO). It's incredibly difficult to get treatment: across 30 European countries, there were 1.4 psychiatrists for every 1,000 prisoners on average, the WHO found. Yet mental health interventions can work. title: Who keeps cooking Europe’s frozen peas?
content: In the early hours of 12 October, a delivery driver pulled up to a French supermarket to find its cold-storage room flooded, with temperatures set to a balmy 50°C. That night, over 700 stores were hacked across the country, and millions of euros' worth of food wasted. Three weeks later, similar attacks targeted retailers in 16 European countries. In France, three blood banks narrowly prevented another disaster thanks to early alarms and intervention systems. Who's coming for our fridges? European and national authorities are struggling to figure out who's behind these attacks, and available evidence is highly disputed. Cybersecurity sources consulted by The European Correspondent said they believe state actors to be the most likely culprits. For one, the hackers never asked for money, and the scale surpasses the capability of a private actor. Cybersecurity company Lupovis runs fake versions of the equipment its clients rely on, including the control systems that run supermarket fridges, as bait for hackers. title: Relax, the embassy of Finland in Canberra is open again
content: Here's something I never thought I'd write: the embassy of Finland in Australia has gone viral. It all started when the Finnish embassy in Canberra announced it would be closed on Tuesday, 10 November, for “an internal planning day” (which turned out to be an end-of-the-year sauna day for the team). Nobody knows why, but the internet lost its mind. Thousands of people all across the world started posting memes on social media about how devastated they were, or how the closure had ruined their day. Like this video with more than 11 million views, or this one joking that riots in Paris were sparked by news of the closure. If you're not familiar with meme culture, the joke is that there is no joke. Nobody actually cares that a small embassy in Canberra is closed for a day (no offence to the staff). The fun is in everyone pretending it's a global catastrophe. But why this particular embassy, and why now? One theory is that the embassy's account was already gaining more attention after a post promoting an all-expenses-paid trip to Finland for 16 singles from across the world, “complete with dinner dates with local Finns” and organised by Finland's national tourism organisation.

title: Europe's invaders have red claws
content: Lake Milada, one of Czechia's largest lakes, is home to a diverse range of animals: European catfish, greylag geese, and smooth snakes. But in September, recreational cyclists came across an unusual sight: a red crayfish marching on the path. While crayfish are not new to the country – signal and spiny-cheek crayfish have displaced native species over the years – this one was different. It was a red swamp crayfish, which is found in freshwater in about 20 European countries, but had never been spotted in Czechia before. Originally from North America, these crayfish are among the most invasive in Europe. For nature conservationist Lenka Čolobentičová and her colleagues at the country's Nature Conservation Agency, it was not good news. “They’re very aggressive; they fight a lot with other crayfish species, they carry the crayfish plague, and they reproduce quickly,” she told The European Correspondent. Though not confirmed, the agency believes it was likely released into Lake Milada by a hobbyist. Across Europe, invasive species are one of the five major causes of biodiversity loss. title: The EU wants to make the internet less shitty
content: “It needs to be nice at first. But then make it shitty,” says the “enshittificator” in a Norwegian Consumer Council video, who explains how companies offering digital services have made the internet less user-friendly. It's satire of “enshittification”, a concept coined by author Cory Doctorow to describe how much of the internet has got less useful or even worse over the years. It taps into growing frustration with online services that use “dark patterns” to nudge people to buy things they may not want, along with addictive design to keep us scrolling. Think of prices you can't find on a website, subscriptions that are incredibly hard to cancel, or warnings that a product is running out so you need to buy it now. Can we clean this up? The European Commission thinks it can, by cracking down on some of these manipulative features. It wants to ban dark patterns and require companies to tell us how to switch off addictive features that encourage compulsive or excessive use. title: Belgium's own ICE could be the first of many in Europe
content: Only 16% of third-country nationals (people not from the EU or EEA) who were ordered to leave Belgium in 2025 actually did so. To raise that number, the Belgian parliament passed the “home raids law” last week. It allows police officers, with authorisation from a judge, to enter private homes and arrest foreign nationals who have refused an order to leave the country and are considered a risk to “public order” or “national security”. In protest against the new measure, 3,000 people formed a human chain around the Palace of Justice in Brussels and demonstrations took place in some 60 municipalities. Activists compare the law to the practices of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). In fact, all of the EU is moving the same way. title: Türkiye is leading climate talks while burning coal
content: COP31 host, Türkiye, is one of the world's 10 largest coal consumers. One of the main themes of the COP31 action agenda is electrification: replacing fossil fuels with electricity in sectors such as transport and industry. But electrification only cuts emissions if the electricity itself is clean, and in Türkiye coal is still the main source of electricity. Türkiye has pledged to speed up electrification, with a proposed national target of raising electricity's share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035. Climate and energy campaigner at Greenpeace Türkiye, Emel Türker Alpay, told TEC the country's coal strategy is a short-sighted way of pursuing energy independence. It's also costly: the government provides around €2.4 billion a year in subsidies and incentives to support coal, aiming to boost domestic output, reduce dependence on energy imports, and protect jobs in coal-producing regions. And because some of that coal is imported, she argued, it does little to make Türkiye energy-independent. And the cost of dependence is rising. title: Europe just can't kick its cookie habit
content: How long do you think people usually spend on a webpage before clicking? If you guessed 41 seconds or less, you get a cookie. Or, well, a couple of dozen. A disproportionate amount of our time online is eaten up dealing with cookie banners. Depending on how it's measured, each interaction takes between five and 23 seconds. In a national survey, 82% of Germans said they found cookie banners annoying. A separate European poll found 39% of users quickly accept cookies just to get rid of them. That may be no coincidence. Experts have long warned that the advertising industry deliberately designs cookie banners to make them difficult to navigate, nudging you into sharing more of your data. And even when we manage to refuse, a study found that up to 65.4% of websites may still collect our data. But cookie banners aren't inevitable. A growing movement is calling for an alternative: setting your preferences once in your browser which would then communicate these choices to websites. The EU has been considering this approach for years. But efforts to introduce it have repeatedly failed during negotiations. In October, a vote by the Council of the EU killed it again, possibly for good. Why?

title: There's a health app for that. Or is there?
content: A friend recently suggested I get a mole on my back checked, just to be safe. As I'm pretty doctor-avoidant (possibly partly a Dutch cultural thing), I remembered the emails my health insurer had been sending me with subject lines like “Check your skin using this smart skin-check app”. I downloaded SkinVision for “unlimited scanning”, fully reimbursed by my insurer. The app promised to tell me “within 30 seconds” whether my mole was dangerous. Once I'd managed to reach the spot with my phone, it delivered its verdict: “low risk”. Great news! An app covered by my health insurer and used by millions of people must be trustworthy, right? Unfortunately, not quite. Earlier this year, researchers at Ghent University and its university hospital published a study assessing SkinVision's accuracy and the university issued a warning. According to the study, the app was wrong in 15% of analyses. It sometimes flagged harmless moles as dangerous and, worse, missed one in four skin cancers. “As a result, many dermatologists are being flooded with harmless moles,” said Niels Chavannes, professor of family medicine at Leiden University who tests health apps for the Dutch National eHealth Living

title: Europe's anti-abortion movement is rich and powerful
content: Six years after Poland's constitutional court imposed a near-total abortion ban on 22 October 2020, thousands of people took to the streets in Warsaw and over 20 other cities. “Women’s hell continues”, read one placard. Abortion is now legal in Poland only in cases of rape, incest, or when a pregnancy poses a threat to the woman's life or health, forcing many women to terminate their pregnancies secretly, or abroad. Today, protesters blame prime minister Donald Tusk’s government for failing to keep its promise to liberalise abortion laws after winning the 2023 election. Although parliament passed two bills in October to ease restrictions – described by activists as “breadcrumbs” – conservative President Karol Nawrocki is expected to veto them. Despite being home to one of the most restrictive abortion laws in Europe, Poland is not the only place where anti-abortion movements are putting reproductive rights at risk. A report by the Centre for Reproductive Rights found that over the past decade, Europe has seen an overall positive trend towards reforms improving access to abortion care. However, in some countries, outdated legal and policy barriers continue to block or delay access.

title: The strange appeal of Spain's useless bar napkins
content: Anyone who's been to Spain will recognise the little white napkins and dispensers found in its bars and restaurants. Try wiping your greasy fingers after eating a jamón croqueta or cleaning up a spilled caña, and you'll quickly discover they're pretty useless. You can easily get through half a dozen and still end up with dirty hands. These flimsy little things, known as servilletas, are an icon of traditional Spanish bar culture. In some places, a floor covered in them is apparently a good sign: it means the place is popular (although the habit has become less common as local authorities have cracked down on littering). But if they're so useless, why do Spanish bars keep using them? I decided to find out. Turns out I've been using them wrong all along. Servilletas are made from sulfite paper. It's not particularly absorbent, but it does resist grease. And that's the whole point. “They're useful because they really are a good barrier against liquids and sauces you can find in saucy sandwiches or saucy tapas,” Alberto García Moyano explained to me. title: Ever dreamt of living in a castle?
content: The housing market has been bad for so long that I am ready to expand my horizons. But rather than turning to the usual suspects, like tiny homes or van life, I'm dreaming big: castles! Turns out there's more to them than I thought. Castles were originally built as fortified dwellings. Fancy homes for royalty and nobility without defensive fortifications are called palaces. And what about fortresses? Think castles built mostly for stationing soldiers – like knights. Of course, we shouldn't forget ruins, which for our purposes are rather uninhabitable. So far, my quest has led me to two insights. Castles dominate western Europe, while palaces are more common in the centre of the continent, and fortresses tend to cluster around historical frontiers. But, more importantly, with the state of natural gas prices, heating a castle would be a nightmare – and I hate being cold.

title: What it takes to get Europe on a bike
content: On 22 September in Turin, Italy, a car driver hit and killed a seven-year-old boy cycling to school. “That could have been me, or my daughter, or anyone, really. Because that place is dangerous,” resident Maria Cristina Caimotto told us. Every morning since then, Caimotto has joined a crowd of people on bikes in the street where the tragedy took place to show solidarity with the family, but also to ask for safer streets and fewer cars. “We cannot erase what happened. We can only do everything we can so that it does not happen again,” she said. Backed by 13 civil society associations, the activists want Turin to move away from its dependence on cars. It’s ambitious, but not impossible: a similar tragedy helped push the Netherlands to become the cycling country it is today. Until the 1970s, the Netherlands was full of cars. In 1971, a six-year-old was killed cycling to school, and her father's newspaper article launched the “Stop de Kindermoord” (Stop the Child Murder) campaign against children dying in traffic. title: Gay sheep don't come cheap
content: “That one flehmened. He wants sex,” farmer Michael Stücke says, pointing to a ram (a male sheep) tilting its head up and curling its upper lip back. This way of smelling the air is known as the flehmen response, which male animals often do before mating. We’re standing in a pasture on Stücke’s sheep farm in the German town of Löhne in North Rhine-Westphalia, observing what looks like a regular flock of sheep. In reality, it may be the world’s most famous: 36 sheep, but they’re all rams, and they’re all gay. Rams that show no interest in mating with ewes (female sheep) and instead pursue other rams are relatively useless to breeders, Stücke says, so they’re usually sent to slaughter. title: Your family's social status still determines yours
content: France, Germany, Portugal, the Netherlands, Italy, and beyond. Young people were once again on the streets across Europe last Saturday. These protests had different triggers, for instance anger over school conditions in France, or opposition to the potential return of conscription in Germany. But there's one shared, underlying frustration: many young people feel that they won't have a better life than their parents. And there are reasons for that feeling. A decades-long development is coming to a head: social mobility has stalled across much of Europe. It refers to the ability to move up – or down – the social and economic ladder – a core promise of liberal democracy. It's mainly measured by occupation, income, and education level. Can someone whose parents never went to university get a degree? Can they find a job that pays better than their parents' work does? Increasingly, the answer to both questions is no. title: Trains are still safe
content: The recent horrific rail accident in Spain was the second such accident in the country within the past year. Those two crashes have already killed more passengers than in the deadly year of 2013, when 97 passengers died in train accidents, according to Eurostat. The number of major rail accidents and fatalities has generally declined in Europe since 1980 – despite a small uptick in recent years. Trains remain one of the safest modes of transport. As a train passenger, your risk of dying in a rail accident is one third that of a bus or coach passenger and very similar to that of a commercial aircraft passenger. By comparison, car occupants are around 40 times more likely to die than train passengers travelling the same distance.

content: Depending on where you live, your waste can take several routes. About half of the waste in the EU gets recycled or composted, the rest ends up either in a landfill or a giant furnace. title: What do Taylor Swift and Giorgia Meloni have in common?
content: Taylor Swift, a billionaire pop empress, and Giorgia Meloni, the far-right Italian prime minister, aren't often mentioned in the same breath. But they're caught in a similar battle, both trying to find new ways to fight an army of AI deepfakes by filing for EU trademarks to protect their voices. Swift's company, TAS Rights Management LLC, wants to register her saying “Hey, it's Taylor Swift”, according to a 6 October filing at the EU Intellectual Property Office. Meloni filed on 5 October to register herself saying “Io sono Giorgia Meloni.” While you can't trademark someone's voice as a whole, these trademarks would give them the exclusive right to their voice saying those words. That could technically stop anyone else from using the voice for a deepfake. Infringing a trademark risks lawsuits and claims for financial damage. It might also be easier to get tech platforms to quickly remove trademark-infringing content. Swift already filed for a US trademark for her voice earlier this year. title: Domestic abuse leaves receipts
content: Your bank statement says a lot about your lifestyle. For women, it could also provide early hints of domestic abuse, according to a recent Nature paper. Using data from Lloyds, the UK's largest retail bank, the study found certain banking patterns in domestic abuse victims' statements as early as seven years before they disclosed their situation. The authors compared more than 5,000 women who had told their bank they were experiencing abuse with over 15,600 customers who had not. Women who disclosed abuse were more likely to have missed a payment, and had lower credit scores. They were also more likely to receive welfare benefits, and their savings were £3,500 lower on average. Their spending patterns also differed: they spent less on self-care, such as the dentist, optician, or sports, and more on alcohol – possibly as a coping strategy, the authors noted. They also spent more on taxis and legal fees. They withdrew cash and changed PIN numbers and address more often, which the authors argue could hint at an abuser taking control of their finances, but also victims regaining it after leaving. title: Rioting for a reason
content: If you've glanced at the news lately, you've probably seen many reports about riots, looting, and violence at protests across Europe. These protests are driven mostly by young people demanding better school conditions and affordable housing, among other things. Yet many headlines focus on violence or riots rather than protestors' demands. Of the more than 10,000 news reports of protests in France by European outlets, just 8% of headlines explicitly mentioned protest demands. Meanwhile, around one in three headlines mentioned terms related to violence. In fact, some of the most-used words in headlines are associated with violence, including “riot”, “clash”, “chaos”, and “violence” itself.

content: It’s 9.30. title: I took a five-star ride to the front line
content: At the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it was still relatively easy to get to Kramatorsk, a city in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk region. I remember my first trip in 2022, by train. I travelled from Kyiv to Kramatorsk on an old Soviet-era train, packed with soldiers and smelling of onions, cold cigarettes, and sweat. Since then, I have used almost every possible way of getting there. By car, bus, Sprinter van, and car rental. But the closer Russian forces moved towards the city, the harder it became to reach. Trains to Kramatorsk stopped running in 2025. content: In May, I bumped into my colleague Tuğba Tekerek at a gathering of Turkish journalists in Istanbul. “Freelancers should come together and look out for one another,” she said. “Sure,” I told her. “Let's brainstorm soon.” We never got the chance. title: All Souls or just your cat's?
content: On All Saints' Day (1 November) and All Souls' Day (2 November), millions of Europeans visit cemeteries and light candles in memory of the dead. But few believe the dead can still reach them. While the dead are remembered in this Christian tradition that dates back to the 10th century, few people today believe the dead can still reach out to the living. But what about animals? A Pew Research survey across 10 countries found that people are often more likely to believe that living animals have spirits than to believe the spirits of their dead ancestors can help or harm them. The gap is the biggest in Türkiye, where 81% believe living animals have spirits while 21% think our ancestors can still reach us. In Spain, most people don't believe in either. So don't forget to light a candle for all our furry friends who are still among us!

title: Frontex is eyeing sweeping new powers
content: The EU's border agency Frontex should take charge of deporting migrants, the European Commission said last week. This would put an agency once accused of serious human rights violations at the heart of enforcing new rules to “return” or expel people who haven't been granted the right to stay in the EU. The tougher EU talk on migration follows a harsher stance from right-wing parties who teamed up earlier this year to agree on the Returns Regulation to detain non-EU nationals who have been ordered to leave. They would then be sent to so-called “return hubs”, such as a centre in Albania for people expelled from Italy who can't be deported to an unsafe home country. Frontex currently cooperates with EU governments to remove people from the EU. It worked with them on some 64,000 returns last year, of which 65% were voluntary and 35% forced. It chartered more than 220 flights and reintegrated some 20,000 people back into their home country, which frequently involves paying them to leave Europe. content: There’s the yellow swallowtail, a large, bright yellow butterfly with a stunning tail. title: Europe is a pumpkin paradise
content: Europe has developed quite an appetite for pumpkins, a crop that isn't native to the continent. More than 1.2 million tonnes were harvested in Europe last year. So how did pumpkins become a Halloween staple? The answer lies in the origins of Halloween, a tradition millions of Scottish and Irish immigrants brought to the United States in the 1800s. They celebrated Samhain, an ancient Celtic festival marking the end of summer and harvest season. To ward off spirits, people hollowed out hard root vegetables like turnips and carved frightening faces into the rind before placing a candle inside. In America, where turnips were scarce, pumpkins offered a convenient alternative. Much easier to carve, they became the defining symbol of Halloween. The tradition has since travelled back across the Atlantic, bringing the pumpkin along with it. Perhaps Europe is taking back Halloween, one pumpkin at a time. Writer’s note: I carved my first pumpkin last weekend, and if that was a struggle, I have no idea how anyone managed to carve a raw turnip without losing a finger.

content: Coal has long been synonymous with Polish energy. Just 20 years ago, 91% of Poland's electricity came from coal. title: Too violent for a war? Perfect for a protest!
content: First, I teared up. Then my nose started itching, and then came the coughs. First from those around me, until I joined the choir myself. The crowd grew uneasy, people looked for a way out, and the chaos began. That's how I experienced tear gas for the first time at a protest in Türkiye in 2025, but it could just as easily describe one of the many protests this month where police used tear gas: be it in Belgium, Italy, Albania, or, most importantly, France. Nowhere has tear gas been used more than in France, the country that gave birth to it. According to data from Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, analysed by The European Correspondent, some 1,520 protests between 2020 and 2026 involved tear gas. title: Raving, reading, and resisting in Ukraine
content: It could be Berlin or New York. One autumn evening, hundreds gather in the rounded hall of a brutalist building at Kyiv Polytechnic Institute. A DJ plays soft electronic music. Go to some of the classes and listen to a lecture about literature. Or simply listen to music and meditate. But in Ukraine, books have become more than a pastime. title: Loans don't grow on trees
content: Ever wondered what tobacco and banks have in common? Very soon, both will be warning consumers about the risks associated with their products. From 20 November, under new EU rules, adverts for consumer credit will have to include a clear and prominent warning: “Caution! Borrowing money costs money.” Very similar to the ones you see on cigarette packets. The requirement to warn consumers that loans don't grow on trees is part of new regulation to protect EU consumers taking out loans. Lenders will also face stricter requirements on the information they provide in credit adverts. This includes the total cost of borrowing and, where applicable, the loan's duration and repayment instalments. Misleading advertising will also be prohibited. The updated rules extend consumer credit protections to small loans of less than €200 and “buy now, pay later” (BNPL) schemes, which have become increasingly common in online shopping. title: How to shut down half a country in 10 days
content: Walking down the aisle of your local supermarket, and all you see are bare shelves and rows of empty boxes. A sign reads: “Delivery not received. Sorry for the inconvenience.” There is no bread, fruit, or vegetables – just frozen food, which you quickly stock up on. This is not a flashback to 2020, when panic-buying for pasta and toilet paper during the Covid-19 pandemic left supermarket shelves emptied. This time, the shortages are linked to workers' protests in southern Italy over soaring fuel prices. It all began with the farmers on 10 October: they called for mass demonstrations in the Italian regions of Calabria, Apulia, Basilicata, and Sicily, and workers in the transport sector immediately joined. Striking hauliers switched off their engines on roads and motorways, and refused to unload their goods. Fishermen also joined the protests, leaving their boats docked at port. title: Less friendly with the rest of the world
content: European national football teams play fewer friendlies against non-European opponents than they used to. The number of friendly games played between a UEFA national team and a team from a different confederation dropped from an average of 55.3 games a year before 2019 to 38.6 after 2019. The drop coincides with the launch of the UEFA Nations League in late 2018. This new competition would replace many of the international friendlies teams used to play. UEFA said the aim was to add “status and appeal to national team football.” The number of intercontinental friendlies varies from year to year. It tends to rise in World Cup years, when teams seek opponents from other continents to prepare for the tournament. The number of friendlies rose in 2026, when 43 of the year’s 67 friendlies against non-European teams were played in June, just before the expanded World Cup kicked off.

title: Serbia is free
content: For most of my life, Serbia was a place that you'd better leave. And so I did. But last night, as I followed election results deep into the night all the way from the Netherlands, I felt that Serbia might be a place to come back to for perhaps the first time in my life. Around 21.30 on election night, former president Aleksandar Vučić conceded that his party SNS, which has been in power for the last 14 years, had lost to the Student List, born out of a protest movement that has shaken Serbia since November 2024. Almost instantly, “Serbia is free” echoed all over social media as city streets erupted in joy and celebration. The police, who had been blocking the street in front of the Republic Electoral Commission and patrolling Belgrade since the morning, began to retreat, and two years of building tension was released in fireworks, chants, and dancing deep into the night. The Student List won by a landslide. title: The Black Sea is turning green, and not the good kind
content: “This summer, we went 38 km deep in the Black Sea. You can see how it is more green,” Martin Tomov, a campaigner for Greenpeace Bulgaria, told us. Satellite images from EUMETSAT confirm his observation. The scientific name for this is eutrophication: an excess of nutrients allows algae to bloom, turning rivers and seas from crystal blue to green. It happens when manure or nitrate- and phosphate-based fertilisers spread on farmland run off into rivers. When the algae later die and rot, they strip the water of oxygen, which suffocates fish, and can also release a poisonous gas. “They also block sunlight; it prevents many organisms from surviving, which impacts the entire food chain,” Tomov told us. In 2016, a jogger died on a beach in Brittany, France, after inhaling poisonous gas from rotten algae. A court held the state liable nine years later, and France compensated his family. But Europe is far from responding adequately. Nearly one third of the EU's rivers, lakes, and coastal waters, and 81% of marine waters, are eutrophic according to an EU report from early this year. title: I See You, ICC
content: The International Criminal Court (ICC) won the EU's human rights prize last week, a big vote of support from the European Parliament for its work in putting war criminals on trial and just 13 days after the US imposed sanctions on the tribunal. But it's “somewhat problematic” for the EU's assembly to award the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought to the court “whilst simultaneously being indecisive and arguably weak regarding its responses to the US sanctions,” said Benjamin Thorne, an assistant law professor at the University of Reading. The Hague-based court, backed by 125 countries, has convicted 15 people to date, all from African countries. It currently has arrest warrants for Russian president Vladimir Putin and Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. title: Man up, don't save the planet
content: Are you a man who cares about the climate? Then you might be a “soy boy” (or for our less chronically online readers: lacking masculine traits). Research suggests that men who want to protect the environment are often seen as warmer and more caring – traits traditionally associated with femininity. Michael Haselhuhn, an associate professor of management at the University of California, published research on this. When asked if they would use cold water for laundry to save money, most men said they would. “When I said it helps the environment because it saves electricity, the support dropped by 10%,” Haselhuhn said. Across most European countries, there is a gender gap in how women and men see environmental issues. Women tend to care more about protecting the environment than men. “In Northern and Western Europe, men are less likely to vote for green parties or parties that emphasise protecting the environment,” said Ingvild Zinober, a researcher studying the green gender gap at the European University Institute. title: Coffeemaxxed lifestyle
content: As a coffee addict, I dream of living in a city where cafés stay open for as much of the day as possible, ideally opening early and closing late. But my past geographical choices haven’t exactly served me well. To find out where I should have settled, I collected Google Maps listings for cafés in about 80 of Europe’s largest cities, covering roughly 15,000 active cafés. The data revealed a few interesting things beyond opening hours. London and Istanbul have the most café listings, but neither scores particularly well in customer reviews. If you’re after the best-rated cafés, Romania is a good choice: Bucharest’s cafés have a median rating of 4.8 out of 5, based on more than 30,000 reviews. For a coffee fanatic like me, the Balkans and Istanbul may be the best bet: cafés in Tirana, Podgorica, Zagreb and Pristina stay open for around 15 hours a day. title: Extremists have no idea what Norse mythology is really about
content: Thor, the Norse god of thunder, once visited the giant Utgard-Loki. The giant challenged him to empty a drinking horn, lift a cat, and wrestle an old woman. He failed all three and left questioning his power. As it turned out, Utgard-Loki had used magic to hide Thor's real opponents. He had been drinking from the ocean, and the cat was Jörmungandr, the gigantic sea serpent encircling the earth. The old lady? Old age itself. This is the Norse myth I remember most clearly. For most people across Scandinavia and Iceland, the old myths don’t play a big role in everyday life, but there are subtle signs of them. Weekdays, streets, and people are named after Norse gods, for instance. Or the countless TV shows, comics, books, and music inspired by old gods and myths. We don't know when and how Norse mythology started, but it was definitely practised in Scandinavia and Iceland in the late Iron Age (from 500 AD) and Viking Age (800-1050 AD). Northern Europe was then gradually Christianised around the year 1000, through missionaries and due to pressure from foreign trade from the south. title: What does the C say about your yoghurt?
content: Let's say you're in a shop looking for yoghurt. You're standing at the fridge, choosing between strawberry and plain. The pots show five letters, running from a dark-green A to a red E. title: Giving Amsterdam's streets a face
content: If you live in a European city, it's likely your street is named after someone. But do you know who that person was, what they did to earn a place on the map, or what they looked like? And all this thanks to a grassroots initiative run by two Amsterdam residents. Geef straten een gezicht (“Give streets a face”) is a project launched by photographer and graphic designer Paul Fennis in 2013. He installs portraits and short biographies to help people understand the history behind their street names. title: Playing by the rules?
content: The strength of courts, rights and checks on power is declining across Europe, reflecting a broader global recession, according to data from the World Justice Project’s Rule of Law Index. The index measures eight factors, including checks on government power, the absence of corruption and the justice system. Since 2021, Europe's average score has fallen in seven of the eight areas, and remained unchanged in one: corruption. Although the declines are small, less than 1.5 points out of 100, they are consistent. Two-thirds of European countries scored lower in 2026 than in 2021. Russia, Belarus, Türkiye and Serbia remain at the bottom of the European rankings, but some of the steepest declines were also recorded in Georgia, Portugal and Slovakia. Europe still scores substantially higher than the global average, and nine of the world's ten highest-ranked countries are European.

title: How to win (and lose) an ally in 10 days
content: These past few weeks mark a more deliberate and open campaign of coercion against Europe and Ukraine by the US and Russia. Both US president Donald Trump and Russian president Vladimir Putin have something to gain: a better result for the Republicans in the upcoming US midterm elections, a Ukraine pushed into defeat, and a Europe that still depends on the US. What happened: 9 October: Trump and Putin hold a long phone call. Afterwards, the US lifts sanctions on Russian diesel until April 2027, letting Russia sell millions of tonnes of it to the US and global markets. Historian Anne Applebaum called it “an abrupt, Hail Mary attempt to force Ukraine to surrender and to save the Russian economy.” Never mind that, according to the EU's economy chief, Russia can't export enough diesel to change prices. On the call, Putin proposes a summit with Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping in China next month to decide Ukraine's future, without Ukraine. content: A supermarket on the outskirts of Copenhagen has become the unlikely site of a futuristic labour experiment. Føtex is training humanoid robots to restock its shelves at night, a task it estimates currently takes 40-50% of its staff's time. One day, they hope to have two high-tech assistants in every store, not to replace employees but to speed up routine tasks, they say. title: Priced out of Netflix
content: When Netflix raised my subscription price again to €17 per month, I paid and moved on. But it made me wonder what the same subscription costs everyone else. title: Do we really need all this cheese water?
content: A spoonful of whey in your morning cereal, a protein shake after an intense leg session. For many of us, focusing on protein in our diets has become a habit. Fewer of us know where the protein taking over our supermarkets actually comes from. Gym-goers' favourite product, whey powder, is a by-product of cheesemaking: it starts as the yellowish liquid left over after milk is thickened into curds and strained. That liquid is then dried into powder. Whey keeps most of milk’s lactose and water-soluble vitamins and about a fifth of its protein. For centuries, people drank it (for example the Scottish whey wine called “blaand“) or used it as a medicine for gut health. Today, up to 200 million tonnes of whey are produced as a by-product of industrial cheesemaking globally. The European Union alone makes more than a quarter of it. title: Elected women never asked to be nudified, yet here we are
content: As a person of a marginalised gender, existing online means being constantly amazed by all the ways the internet can be used against you, no matter how powerful you are. One of the latest additions to that arsenal are “nudification” apps, AI-powered tools that can be prompted to create fake, sexually explicit pictures and videos of people, usually without their consent. title: Your fries are getting shorter (but no less crispy)
content: No matter what the weather did to this year's harvest, Belgium will still deliver its biggest contribution to the culinary cultural canon: fries. They will still taste good. But this season, the long ones may be missing from your paper cone. First came the potato glut. Last year’s harvest was so abundant that potatoes sold without a contract went for between €0 and €5 per 100 kg – far below production costs, said Daniel Ryckmans, an agronomist at the Walloon potato organisation FIWAP. For this season, the sector asked farmers to plant less, and they did: Belgium's potato fields shrank by 17.4%. Then the summer came, and multiple extreme heatwaves came with it. “This year there was not enough rain. And above that, it was too hot,” Ryckmans told us. title: European businesses are keen to go green
content: The EU has a favourite word: competitiveness. To better compete in the global economy, the European Commission is rewriting (and often weakening) environmental rules for businesses, for example to reduce reporting burdens. Making life easier for our biggest industries sounds reasonable: we shouldn't impose rules that drive them out of business, should we? Yet what do businesses actually want? A recent GlobeScan survey commissioned by the environmental group WWF asked 350 European business leaders. Only 29% said the EU's environmental simplification efforts have helped them, while 55% reported a negative or mixed impact. Meanwhile, 91% said shifting to a low-carbon economy will make Europe more competitive in the long run. Some of that frustration comes from companies that moved towards sustainability first. Many invested in line with the Commission's own green rules, and now feel punished by the uncertainty of changing rules. title: Stamps worth more than your house
content: If you've never thought long and hard about stamps, you are most certainly not a philatelist – a student or collector of postage history. During the stamp craze of the mid-19th century, the French spoke about “timbromanie”, or the mania of rabid philatelist collectors. Who would've thought that humble postage stickers would unleash such heated passion among Europe's well-to-do? The most valuable stamps in the world are mostly the freaks among them, including those printed in the wrong colour or displaying their subject upside down. Others are famous for their lore, like the improvised “1856 British Guiana 1-Cent Magenta” (the second stamp in the visual), printed by British colonists after the Crown failed to send them a new batch in time. As such, stamps have always been as much about power as they are about mail. Colonial and imperial rulers used them to thrust their faces into the daily lives of people; Poland and Czechoslovakia, once independent, reissued stamps from elsewhere by printing right over them.

title: The Amazon of Europe is going thirsty
content: “Look at that!” exclaimed conservationist Jasmin Sadiković, as he steered his small metal boat through the Croatian heart of the five-nation (Austria, Slovenia, Croatia, Hungary, and Serbia) UNESCO Mura-Drava-Danube biosphere reserve. Known as the Amazon of Europe for the scale of its wilderness, the reserve stretches across some of the continent's most valuable river landscapes. Sadiković was pointing at sandbanks that are usually underwater. After a hot, dry summer, water levels in the Drava river had fallen to record lows. The exposed banks had been in the sun so long that grass and shrubs were beginning to grow. “I've never experienced such conditions,” said Sadiković, “and I was born on the banks of the river.” Indeed, his hometown Osijek has a maternity ward that overlooks the river, and the extroverted Croatian has spent most of his 52 years living alongside it, swimming and fishing in its waters. For decades now, he's been working to protect it with the NGO Green Osijek, which he joined the year it was founded, in 1995. title: Europeans win, abroad
content: When Belgian physicist Francis Halzen was awarded this year’s Nobel prize in Physics, he became the ninth European among the past 10 physics laureates. But Halzen, who won his prize while working at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, is also part of a less celebrated trend. Four of those nine Europeans carried out the research that earned them the prize outside their home countries, mostly in the United States. The trend runs across all scientific Nobel categories (physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, and economics), where European laureates are increasingly likely to have done their prize-winning work abroad. It is most pronounced in economics, where more than two-thirds of European winners did their Nobel-recognised research at a foreign university. In physics and chemistry, the share is more than a third. The Nobel prize reflects a wider brain drain with European researchers leaving for better-funded positions elsewhere. The EU is trying to bring dissatisfied or laid-off American researchers to Europe through its “Choose Europe for Science” initiative. title: Who owns Albania?
content: Protesters are still waving pink flamingos on wooden poles, over four months into their movement. As they march through the streets in central Albania they chant ”Rama in jail, Berisha in jail,” referring to the prime minister and the opposition leader. title: Want to ditch your gas boiler? Ask your city
content: You may never have worried about the Strait of Hormuz, had it not been for the impact on your wallet, right? With gas prices hitting record highs and fossil fuels contributing to climate change, perhaps it's finally time to say goodbye to the old gas boiler in the bathroom? Hmmm... What seems like an easy choice on paper can be a much harder one in practice. Whether we can make the switch, and when, depends on the alternatives available where we live, how much money we need to invest and whether public support is available to help us go greener. Your local government has a big influence on all three. Local politicians can make practical decisions about heat networks and building renovation. They are also closer to residents, which makes them best equipped to identify people affected by energy poverty and target support where it is needed most. That's precisely what Greenpeace decided to track: they followed 15 European cities and assessed how well they're doing in the green heating race (or whether they are racing backwards). title: Four broken promises are fuelling young people's anger
content: France, Belgium, Spain, Albania – young people have taken to the streets across Europe in recent weeks. Their grievances are different – school conditions, housing, or corrupt governments. Many of these protests reflect a shared frustration: the feeling that Europe's politics is failing to deliver for the next generation. A 2026 survey showed that just over half of 16- to 26-year-olds in Europe are optimistic about their future, down from 70% in 2017. First broken promise: education In France, the ongoing student protests were sparked by poor school conditions, teacher shortages, and overcrowded classrooms. It's a common problem across European countries: in Germany, municipalities report a €68.9 billion backlog in school building repairs. title: A year of fruits
content: We recently published a story asking what eating seasonally even means. Fruit likes to make that question even trickier. title: EU governments are sweating over trade with China
content: For years, China has been selling far more to EU customers than it buys in return. The EU imported nearly €54 billion worth of goods in July, while exporting only €17.4 billion. That's a difference of €36.5 billion, or more than €1 billion a day flowing from EU countries to China. Over the past decade, that deficit has more than doubled in value as the EU keeps buying more from China, increasingly higher-value goods. European manufacturers and retailers complain that they can no longer compete with Chinese rivals who sell their products for far less, partly thanks to government subsidies that help cover their costs. Lower exports and sales of EU goods hurt the EU economy and can put EU companies out of business. This kind of trade imbalance “is unsustainable,” European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said in a speech last month. “It shows in our communities and in factories across our Union. title: “Throw us some teachers, not tear gas”
content: Dinosaurs, unicorns, and Spidermen are still protesting on French streets, alongside live brass bands, teachers having “aura battles” with their students, and signs that read “throw us some teachers, not tear gas” or “I wish I was as hot as my classroom”. content: Over four days last week, Ukrainian drones hit data centres run by Yandex, known as “Russia's Google”. Soon after, claims spread that bot traffic online had gone down. title: Will tiny viruses rescue us?
content: You can’t see them, but bacteriophages are on your skin, in wastewater, and in the depths of our oceans. Wherever there are bacteria, there are bacteriophages – or phages, for short. These small viruses are the natural enemies of bacteria and they outnumber all other living organisms combined. “We consist of more bacteriophages and bacteria than our own cells,” Kārlis Rācenis, vice-dean of sciences at Riga Stradiņš University’s Faculty of Medicine, explained. He researches phages and is – in his own words – a “phage enthusiast”. Phage research is having a revival as an increasingly promising way to tackle multi-drug resistant (MDR) infections as bacteria become more resistant to antibiotics. Every year, about 35,000 people in the EU/EEA die due to antimicrobial resistance (AMR), the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) estimates based on data from 2020. Despite being discovered in 1917, eleven years before antibiotics, phage therapy is still considered experimental due to a lack of randomised clinical trials. So what can we expect? title: When food becomes too political
content: Good news for Asterix fans: the banquet is making a comeback in rural France. Think of the grand feasts at the end of the Asterix comics, where villagers gather around long tables to eat, drink and celebrate. A French company called Le Canon français is bringing that spirit to life, organising large-scale banquets across the country, each attracting between 1,000 and 3,000 people. Tickets cost around €80 and include four courses of local food and some wine. Guests sit at long communal tables, usually in a rented warehouse or event hall. title: In Amsterdam, you can ring a doorbell to test your drugs
content: After meeting his dealer, Peter (not his real name) hunts for a doorbell in one of Amsterdam's narrow alleys. “Drug service”, reads the label underneath the button. “I'm here to test some drugs,” Peter says into the intercom, and the door opens. Inside, a few people wait silently on plastic chairs, and leaflets are scattered across a table. About 20 minutes later, it's Peter's turn. He gets called to a different room to test his cocaine. Peter has walked into one of the paradoxes of Dutch drug policy: buying and possessing drugs such as cocaine is illegal, yet testing them is allowed as part of a government-supported system. A network of 34 locations has been checking drugs across the country for over 30 years. It's a similar construction to the famous Dutch weed policy: possessing cannabis is technically illegal but “gedoogd” (tolerated) in many cases. The testing locations follow the Dutch policy that completely stopping drug use is impossible, and that adding measures to reduce harm, besides prevention, is beneficial to protect public health. content: On Tuesday morning, two Turkish-owned ships sailing under the flags of Palau and Togo were attacked by drones off the coast of Bulgaria. title: Europe's skies are buzzing with mystery drones
content: Between 1 January 2025 and early October 2026, there were more than 200 reported drone incursions within NATO airspace, including sightings, interceptions, and the discovery of drone debris – according to our analysis based on media and government reports, an overview by Heiko Pleines of the University of Bremen, and droneincidents.eu. Drone incidents include sightings over airports and critical infrastructure, and belong to growing incidents of hybrid warfare in Europe that also include sabotage, arson, and influence operations. title: Spare some change for the EU?
content: The EU had a budget of just under €150 billion to spend last year, less than Denmark's. This covered payouts to farmers and researchers, humanitarian aid, and salaries for its civil servants. Around two-thirds of that money comes from EU member state governments, who contribute based on the size of their economies. But the EU also raises some of its own income, or “own resources”, which includes a small slice of the value-added tax (VAT) on what we buy, a levy on plastic waste, and part of the customs duties on imports. And it wants more. The EU has big bills to pay in the coming years – as much as €30 billion a year in repayments for its €800 billion Covid-19 recovery fund. It's also got big ambitions for what it could do with more money to fund defence, energy independence, and breakthrough technologies. title: When missiles strike, Ukrainians turn to their phones
content: A first missile hits. Then a second, then a third. The walls shake and car alarms, triggered by the blasts, mix with the sound of air raid sirens outside. title: What does eating seasonally even mean?
content: Let me take you into my mother’s basement. Past a heavy door that keeps out summer heat and winter frost, down the stairs, is a dimly lit room full of earthy smells and treasure. The shelves are lined with jars in every shade, from bright green to aubergine: jams, kompots, courgette, tomato and cabbage salads, fermented and pickled cucumbers, alongside berry and apple juice and whatever else my mother has decided to experiment with. There are also boxes of potatoes, carrots, beetroot and apples. Everything here comes from the garden above. This is the old-school way of eating seasonally in the Baltics: eating food fresh while it grows, and preserving it for when it doesn't – in winter. But a supermarket in Rīga sells fresh strawberries and tomatoes all year round. title: Please join the EU, but behave!
content: Joining the EU is a long, hard trek for would-be members. Montenegro, which is closest to joining, has been negotiating for more than a decade. Now, the EU wants to update its terms and conditions for new members. If a country misbehaves, it could lose its funding or even its vote on EU decisions. Harsh words. Their real audience seems to be the EU's existing members, who need convincing that enlarging the club is a good idea after 16 years of Viktor Orbán's Hungary thumbing its nose at EU laws and values. title: 12 Europeans walk into Oktoberfest
content: It’s 15.25 outside the Schottenhamel Festzelt, the oldest Oktoberfest beer tent in Munich, with space for around 9,000 people. A small crowd of women in dirndls (traditional Alpine dresses) of varying sleeve-puffiness and neckline depth, and men in assorted shades of brown leather shorts, is getting shifty. Oktoberfest, or Wiesn as the locals call it, is the world's biggest folk festival. Abroad, it's the quintessential German tradition, but most Germans will point out it's mostly Bavarians celebrating Bavaria. I'm here with 11 other 20-somethings from around Europe, and we've all dressed the part. The sleeve-puffiness of my own dirndl is off the charts. I feel like a 19th-century milkmaid. 16.27 We're among the lucky ones: we have a table and benches from which to drink beer by the litre from “Maß” jugs at €15.80 each. “Oktoberfest is about coming together,” Annika, 25, from Munich, yells over the sound of the live band. “I’ve been going since I was 14. All my friends who left the city come back this time of the year. You walk through the tent and see people you know, and you just hug them.” This year cracked the all-time record of Oktoberfest visitors in Munich at 7.4 million.

title: The fungal networks hiding beneath our feet
content: Something massive is hiding underground: large networks of tiny threads, each many times thinner than a hair. If laid out end to end, they would stretch about 110 quadrillion kilometres – roughly 730 million times the distance from Earth to the sun. These tiny threads are fungi, specifically mycorrhizal fungi. You may think of fungi as mushrooms, but these ones live mostly underground. “Underneath your foot, you might have hundreds of metres of these fungal threads,” Justin Stewart, an evolutionary ecologist and postdoctoral fellow at the Society for the Protection of Underground Networks (SPUN), told us. Stewart is the lead author of a recent study published in Science, used by SPUN to create the first-ever global map of mycorrhizal fungi. These fungi are fantastic biological partners to plants. title: Never been to a protest? You'll still feel the crackdown
content: Civic space is one of those things you won't notice until it's gone. The United Nations defines it as “the environment that enables people and groups to participate meaningfully in the political, economic, social and cultural life of their societies.” Measuring civic space is as much about laws as it is about vibes: besides the legal rights guaranteeing free speech, freedom of assembly, protest, or protection from hate speech, it's also about feeling at ease in exercising these rights – like going to a protest without a mask in case there's tear gas, or an umbrella in case there's a water cannon. content: The EU promised to sanction Israeli ministers and partially suspend the EU-Israel trade agreement in September 2025. Neither has happened. Why? title: The housing crisis just ended the Spanish government
content: What happened: Less than two weeks ago, Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was evicted from the flat in Madrid she had lived in for over 70 years, after the building’s new owner, a real estate company called Urbagestión, raised her rent from €500 to €2,650. Her case sparked outrage over the situation in Spain’s housing market, where even a couple with wages well above the average cannot afford to buy or rent a place on their own. Mass protests across the country pressured prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s government to issue two decrees to prevent cases such as Maricarmen’s, by limiting rent increases and banning real estate companies from buying more flats, among other things. Both failed to secure sufficient support in parliament and were rejected last Friday. On Monday, Sánchez called a snap general election for 29 November. “We have had to contend with very powerful economic and social elites who do not stand for election,” Sánchez said, indirectly referring to alleged lobbying efforts by real estate companies to have the decrees repealed. title: Taxing wealth can be expensive
content: “Tax the rich” is a rallying cry for some to raise government revenue, but the Netherlands actually loses money on its household capital income tax. Governments tax the money a household makes from what it owns – its capital income, which includes returns on savings and investments, and rental income, among other things. Some countries, like France and Luxembourg, raise a relatively high portion (4.5%) of their tax revenue this way. Others, like Slovakia (0.4%) and Malta (0.3%), rely less heavily on taxing household capital to fill their treasury. The Netherlands (-0.9%) breaks the scale by giving away more tax breaks for homeowners than it collects via household capital income tax. That tax relief increases people's borrowing capacity for a mortgage, leading to higher housing prices. As a result, renters end up effectively subsidising homeowners: all taxpayers, regardless of whether they own capital or a home themselves, help fill the gap left by this scheme.

title: French teens are taking on the state
content: A burning building, charging police officers and witty slogans disappearing in a haze of tear gas: high schoolers are protesting all over France. Mass demonstrations have taken place all week. What's going on? On 21 September, teachers at a high school in the Paris suburbs went on strike to protest working conditions. Their students blocked their school to support them, and several other schools in the area followed suit. It eventually spread to other parts of the country. By 4 October, over 5,000 students had been arrested, most of them under 18, since the start of the protests. Hundreds of schools had to close down after a few days, with students attending classes from home. Nearly 200 were injured after riot police were deployed, according to Monday's estimates by the minister of education. For striking students, the protest is a fight to get the education they were always promised but never given. That starts with getting the right number of teachers. In September, 53% of French secondary and high schools started the year short of at least one teacher, according to the country's leading union. Just over 7% of teaching hours could not take place in 2025 due to absent teachers.

content: Of course not. But you might be able to get more people to care about it. title: Is the sky the limit?
content: “Fewer planes, more life,” read one of the banners carried by protesters in Barcelona a couple of weeks ago. Together with demonstrators in the Balearic Islands, they were opposing airport expansions that would bring even more tourists to already overcrowded places. Four of the 12 airports that Spanish operator Aena plans to expand – including Barcelona airport – already account for 66% of the country’s CO₂ emissions from departing flights, according to a report by Transport and Environment (T&E), a clean transport NGO. The report states that aviation emissions in Spain had risen above pre-pandemic levels by 2025, the fastest increase among European markets. T&E analysed plans to expand 20 airports across 10 European countries. Together, the projects would add 225 million tonnes of CO₂ to current emissions – roughly equivalent to Spain's annual emissions – complicating Europe's efforts to reach carbon neutrality by 2050. title: Forever chemicals are in our blood
content: “Cognitive dissonance” is when you hold two conflicting views. Or keep doing something even though you know it conflicts with your beliefs. It's not really a surprise to me that there's chemical pollution around me. I can smell car fumes and see plastic lying in the grass on my way to work. Local ponds and streams are often choked with algae in a region struggling with excess nitrate from agricultural fertilisers. But do I shun plastic? Only buy organic food? Ensure there are absolutely no potentially problematic chemicals in my home? Nope. It's easier to do nothing when you don't really know what you're facing. But that wilful blindness had to end when the European Parliament's Green-EFA group asked me to be one of 110 volunteers from nine countries to get our blood tested for PFAS, or per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances. title: Young women and men are drifting apart politically
content: A trend is gripping many of Europe's democracies: young men are increasingly voting for right-wing parties, while young women are moving further left. In Sweden's September election, 22% of men aged 18 to 30 voted for the far-right Sweden Democrats, compared with half as many women. Young women, meanwhile, vote much further left. In Berlin's recent state election, which was won by the left party, just over half of women under 25 voted for the party, compared to 34% of men. In Poland, the gap is especially stark: 26.3% of men aged 18 to 29 voted for the far-right Confederation party in 2023. title: Winter is coming, are we ready?
content: As temperatures across Europe begin to fall back into the single digits, the region is facing an unenviable challenge: how to get through the colder months with gas reserves at record lows and prices at record highs? EU-wide gas storage was about 70% full in late September – the lowest level recorded in the EU in at least fifteen years for this time of year. This is a result of tighter global liquified natural gas (LNG) supplies amid the US-Israel war on Iran, as well as the EU's decision to relax its gas storage targets last year. The rules were originally introduced in response to the 2022 energy crisis – following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The demand for gas-generated electricity was also higher than usual this summer as extreme heatwaves forced some power plants to reduce or suspend operations. While solar power helped meet the surge in daytime electricity demand from air conditioning, gas was relied upon more heavily in the evenings, explained Chris Rosslowe, energy analyst at the energy think tank Ember. title: Drink a cup of coffee and I'll tell you your future
content: Today is International Coffee Day, so we have to ask: is there a more European drink than coffee? Europeans drink more coffee per capita than anywhere else in the world, on average. And across the continent, coffee has taken on countless forms – from the Italian cappuccino and Irish coffee, to the Greek frappé. But coffee in Europe is about more than what we put in the cup. title: Getting back with the ex?
content: What happened: The UK could think about getting back together with the EU after a bad decade since the break-up, British prime minister Andy Burnham told BBC radio on Wednesday. It's just one of several “options that need to be considered,” he said. Why it matters: None of the six (!) other British leaders since the 2016 vote to leave the EU have seriously mentioned rejoining the bloc. Burnham's predecessor Keir Starmer had promised to rebuild relations with the EU, the country's largest trading partner. But his and Burnham's Labour party had “red lines” that forbade a return to the EU's single market, freedom of movement, or even an alternative arrangement, like the customs union which allows Türkiye to sell many products to the EU without paying tariffs.
