title: The missing votes
content: While EU citizens can move freely and settle anywhere within the Union, they cannot vote in national elections where they live, unless they are also citizens of that country. Though mobile EU citizens can vote in municipal elections and can also run for the European Parliament in their country of residence, an estimated 11.8 million of them have no say in national elections there. If mobile Europeans could vote, they'd likely have a significant influence on electoral outcomes in their host countries. One reason is that they tend to be younger than the local population, according to our analysis of data from Eurostat. Although mobile Europeans generally retain the right to vote in their country of citizenship, research and survey data consistently show that citizens living abroad vote less. Distance, bureaucratic hurdles, and a gradual disconnect from the politics of a country they no longer live in, all contribute to lower turnout. As a result, millions of mobile Europeans may be effectively falling out of democratic participation altogether.

title: The blood grain train rolling through the Baltics
content: Trainload after trainload of “blood grain” is crossing Latvia's eastern border. This is what locals are calling Russian grain, which has found a new route to the Baltic Sea after Ukrainian attacks disrupted the standard route through the Black Sea. Though many Latvians reject the idea of allowing Russian products that could help Moscow fund its war on Ukraine to pass through, the route is completely legal. The EU deliberately left Russian agriculture and food products out of its sanctions, arguing that restrictions could worsen global food security, particularly in developing countries. In 2024, the EU did set tariffs high enough to keep Russian grain off the European market, but made an exception for grain passing through on its way to other countries. Russia is one of the world's largest wheat exporters. Ukraine is making that grain machine sputter. In August, it struck Novorossiysk, Russia's main Black Sea port, knocking out three major grain terminals and disrupting crucial routes: last season, almost 90% of Russia's seaborne grain exports went through the Black Sea. title: Why the world thinks all Germans wear lederhosen
content: Oktoberfest is in full swing in Munich, running until Sunday 4 October. Last year, some 6.5 million people flocked to the festival, including a large share of international visitors (21%). The festival is known around the world, and Oktoberfest-style events have popped up everywhere, arguably making it the most famous German cultural export “product”. What most people don't know is that Oktoberfest is just one of thousands of regional Volksfeste (folk festivals) held across Germany throughout the year. And no, they're not just about beer. Beer tents are usually part of the deal, but so are fairground rides like carousels, Ferris wheels, and rollercoasters, along with travelling fairground businesses, market stalls, and other entertainment. Many began centuries ago as church fairs, agricultural celebrations, horse races, shooting festivals, or sailing regattas. title: Who pays for pricier carbon? You, until the help arrives
content: If you heat your home and fill up your car with gas, oil, or coal, your bills are likely going up from 2028. The EU’s new carbon pricing system, the Emissions Trading System 2 (ETS2), will make fossil fuel suppliers pay for the emissions from the fuel they sell, and they’ll pass that cost on to you. For most households, the increase in heating costs will be modest at around €60 a year on average, according to estimates from the Bertelsmann Foundation. But in Poland, households heating with oil, gas, or coal could pay €372 more each year. The hardest hit are often older homeowners in Slovakia, Hungary, Romania, and Poland, living on around half the average income in their countries. They already spend about 6% of their income on heating, and ETS2 could push that above 7%. Three in four buildings in the EU are energy inefficient, so they use more energy than necessary and every price rise costs them more. At an EU-wide renovation rate of around 1% a year, most won't be fixed any time soon. The EU is offering a safety net for the people hit hardest by ETS2: the Social Climate Fund. title: Estonia is crisis-proofing, and it starts in a gym
content: As far as (unofficial) national mottos go, “fortune favours the prepared” would be a fitting one for Estonia. After centuries of occupation and oppression, few countries seem to be as prepared for Russian aggression as Estonia. On a sunny day in June, this readiness was rehearsed in the town of Rapla, an hour south of Tallinn. In its main sports hall, Triinu Maandi and a handful of other women set up sleeping bags, bedding, and supplies for 350 people. Maandi and roughly 4,000 fellow volunteers of the Women’s Voluntary Defence Organisation would work alongside professional emergency responders in the event of a military conflict. “Given our history, it's a miracle that we can speak Estonian,” Maandi told us. “What came after Soviet [occupation] at the beginning of the 90s was a wreck. So we are trying to do what we can to prevent that from happening again.” Rapla’s sports hall is one of 340 evacuation sites across Estonia, with a combined capacity for approximately 70,000 people. title: Forgot what you walked into a room for? Blame the door
content: We've all experienced it: you walk into a room, and all of a sudden your mind goes blank. What on earth did you go in there to do? That annoying little brain fart has a name: the doorway effect. A new study in the journal Brain and Environment may have come one step closer to figuring out why it happens: when we move from one room to another, there’s an increase in theta activity in the brain. Theta waves are one of five types of brain waves, which are electrical currents measurable through electrodes on the scalp. “Many things in the brain are associated with this theta response,” co-author Zakaria Djebbara told us: memory, spatial awareness, and the brain’s map of the body, for example. Djebbara is an associate professor at Aalborg University in northern Denmark and researches how architecture affects the brain. “The reason we forget might be because the brain resets the understanding of the environment the moment we walk through the door,” Djebbara explained. In the study, electrodes measured the brain activity of 20 participants as they walked through virtual rooms. title: Good news for the planet, bad news for Norway
content: Norway has a green reputation, but it's one of the world's largest exporters of oil and gas, and the EU is its main customer. That could change: the EU is upholding a ban on new oil and gas drilling in the Arctic, despite heavy lobbying from Oslo. Norway has become the Union’s largest gas supplier since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, providing roughly a third of its imports. Most of that gas comes from the North Sea, but some already flows from the Arctic, where Norway has produced gas since 2007 and opened its northernmost oil field last year. The country's production is forecast to decline after 2027 unless new reserves are found, most of which are expected in the northern Barents Sea. title: The how-to guide for turning nature into a border guard
content: It's called “The Game”. The perilous journey migrants take through the Balkans in the hope of reaching the European Union. The 931 kilometre-long border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and EU member state Croatia is one of its focal points. “This border runs across steep mountains, vast rivers, and through dense forests,” Tristan Solf of the Border Violence Monitoring Network (BVMN) told The European Correspondent (TEC). title: Solarpunk could be the future we actually want
content: Morning light filters through houses draped in climbing plants. Rooftops hum with solar panels, and the air feels cooler in the shade of thousands of trees. This dream vision represents solarpunk. It imagines a future that pushes back against decades of dystopian climate narratives. The definition of solarpunk is evolving, but scholars tend to agree that it is positive, progressive and communal. You have probably already encountered it in your everyday life – in video games, music or advertising. Bits of it can be identified in science fiction series like Star Trek, anime like Castle in the Sky, or even Disney movies such as Tomorrowland. A real-life example is the residential Vertical Forest in Milan. You just didn't know it was solarpunk. Solarpunk emerged in dialogue with the more conflictual genres of cyberpunk and steampunk. title: Berlin got hacked, and it shouldn't have been this easy
content: Headlines this month about Germany’s historic far-right win eclipsed another equally grim local record: nearly 6 terabytes of data from Berlin’s digital archives were leaked onto the dark web, in the country’s largest public administration hack to date. The files reportedly contain information on civil servants, private citizens and key infrastructure, including logins, contracts, payslips, medical records and ID copies. title: AI is taking over ... the internet
content: The next time you see a typo in an online article or webpage, don't get annoyed – it might be a sign that an actual human wrote it. According to a recent analysis by the Pew Research Center, over one third of webpages published since the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022 were written with the help of AI. Using a random sample of 10,000 webpages, researchers concluded that 9.6% of all pages ever published show “significant signs of AI editing or authorship.” As LLMs have become widely available, writing has become cheap. Their output is rewriting a resource most of us rely on every day: the internet. Writing is difficult because it pushes you to think, which in turn helps to make up your mind. When we outsource that process to machines, and increasingly consume text produced by them, we risk losing out on our ability to think critically. But we're also surrendering our (potentially) greatest encyclopaedia of all time to non-human “thought” without quite knowing what comes after. At the risk of tooting our own horn, human-written journalism is one tool to keep this from happening. Typos andall.

title: The drone war never sleeps in Kyiv
content: For the past four years, Kyiv has lived by an unwritten rule of war: survive the night, and life can return to normal in the morning. That started to change at the end of August. Between 27 August and 1 September, Kyiv spent 60 hours under air-raid alerts, an unprecedented stretch since Russia launched its full-scale invasion. Three weeks later, those days look less like an exceptionally bad week and more like the beginning of a new normal. This escalation marks a new development in Russia’s drone campaign. title: We can still refreeze the climate ice cube
content: “If you take an ice cube out of the freezer and put it on the table, it starts to melt. If you put the ice cube back in the freezer quick enough, it will freeze again,” climate scientist Nico Wunderling tells me. “But if you wait too long, it will melt entirely before you put it back, and you can’t put the water back into the cube form.” He’s explaining climate tipping points, his area of research at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research and Goethe University Frankfurt. Tipping points are thresholds where a small rise in warming triggers a self-reinforcing feedback loop that becomes very hard to reverse. Think of the melting Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets as giant versions of the melting ice cube. As ice sheets melt and shrink, their surfaces move into warmer air at lower elevations, causing them to melt even faster. This creates a self-reinforcing cycle: the more the ice melts, the warmer the air around it becomes, accelerating further melting. This commits them to near-total collapse over centuries, raising sea levels by metres. But these ice cubes can be refrozen, if they’re put back into the freezer fast enough. title: The EU's plan to childproof the internet
content: Last week, the European Commission unveiled its KIDS Act, a plan that would change how children under 15 interact with the internet across the EU. Over the past two years, nearly all member states have considered some form of age restriction on social platforms. The Commission’s proposal would override this potential patchwork of national laws with one EU-wide rule. This is not simply a social media ban, though. The proposal is much broader. It essentially regulates access to some digital services considered particularly “bad for children” while also requiring companies to make them safer by design. New rules for the new kids on the bloc The KIDS Act applies to seven types of platforms: social media, video-sharing, online games, app stores, operating systems, AI chatbots and AI companions – albeit in different ways. For social media and video-sharing platforms, the proposal creates an age ladder: no accounts under 13, “mini accounts” for 13- and 14-year-olds. These capped profiles would have to be set up by parents and come with a one-hour daily usage limit. Teens could then roam on a brand new, “safer-by-design” version of the internet. title: Protected on paper, burning in practice
content: In wildfire seasons between 2015 and 2025, protected nature around the size of Montenegro burned in Europe, according to The European Correspondent's analysis of data from the European Data Journalism Network. That's 1.3 million hectares, or almost 2% of Europe's protected areas under Natura 2000, a network of protected nature sites across the EU. These areas are disproportionately affected by wildfires. Though they only make up 18.6% of European land, around 29% of the area that has burned over the past 11 years was protected under Natura 2000. Portugal's on-land Natura 2000 areas were most affected, with 13% having burned at some point between 2015 and 2025. Over 3% of the area covered by Natura 2000 burned in Spain, Greece, and Hungary each. In August 2023, a 16-day-long megafire in Evros in northern Greece burned around 96,600 hectares of which 65% was part of a Natura 2000 area. In some cases, this land burns over and over. title: Climate disasters are expensive. Guess who's paying?
content: “Everything has burnt down. It was a big house on a lovely little plot. It had a swimming pool, and it’s burnt down,” a woman from Villa del Prado in Madrid said, in tears, to the Spanish public broadcaster in July. Her plot was devastated after the largest wildfire in Spain's history, which burnt 77,000 hectares. Almost two months later, there is still no official toll of the losses caused by the flames in central Spain, but the European Environment Agency (EEA) has estimated that the direct economic damage in the EU due to weather-related disasters reached €822 billion between 1980 and 2024. One quarter of this loss happened in the last four years. Floods were responsible for almost half of the total cost. “The climate related risks are real and their macroeconomic impact is increasing,” Georg Zachmann, senior fellow at the Brussels-based think tank Bruegel, told The European Correspondent. title: Solar power with a side of strawberries
content: Nicolas Etchelecu will soon be taking over his parents' strawberry farm in the south of France. Their family business has transformed rapidly in the last couple of years. In 2022, they started building a new 3,000-sq-metre greenhouse with a roof made of solar panels: a first of its kind in France. These are “smart” panels: when built-in sensors detect too much sunlight, the panels close automatically to create shade and protect the strawberry plants from excessive heat. When the weather is favourable, and the plants need direct sun, the sensors open the shades. That way, the solar panels help protect the plants from extreme heatwaves, like the ones that hit France this summer, while generating clean electricity at the same time. This new approach to combining farming and solar power is called “agrivoltaics”. Across Europe, agri-panels could create the capacity of up to 51 TW – enough to generate 25 times more than the total current electricity demand in Europe. “The potential of this technology is almost unlimited,” Jiří Bím, a Czech agrivoltaics researcher, told The European Correspondent. title: Back to university, unless you're from Gaza
content: Salwa Abu Elhaj is 23 years old and lives in a tent in Gaza with her parents and siblings. Had everything gone to plan, she would now be at the KU Leuven campus to start her master's in communication science, for which she was awarded a scholarship. Salwa is one of a group of 13 students and researchers from Gaza with scholarships to study in Belgian universities in Antwerp, Brussels, Hasselt, and Leuven. None of them have appeared on campus so far. “I never imagined that I would have to fight this hard just to reach a university that had already accepted me,” Salwa told The European Correspondent. The federal government of Belgium hasn't helped the students apply for a visa in a Belgian consulate, nor has it been willing to organise a diplomatic evacuation. What's stopping them isn't the students' status or the logistics of leaving Gaza, but political bargaining over migration. Belgium's government couldn't reach an agreement on the issue. title: Going far right?
content: Support for far-right parties across Europe has increased in recent years. Added up across the continent, they won 23.5% of votes in the five countries that held parliamentary elections in 2025, and 23.2% in seven countries in 2026, according to PopuList, a peer-reviewed list of populist, far-right, far-left, and Eurosceptic parties. Support for these parties started taking off after 2015, increasing from around 5-6% in the 1990s. However, a few recent examples show that Europe is not moving in just one direction. Hungary and Poland, two former far-right strongholds, elected more moderate governments in their last elections. And the recent Swedish election delivered an upset too. Support for Sverigedemokraterna fell, dropping the far-right party to third place.

title: The fish skin that becomes one with your body
content: Guðmundur Fertram Sigurjónsson, an inventor and CEO originally from a small Icelandic fishing village, was looking at fish scales for wound healing, and realised fish skin is structurally similar to human skin. And this makes it an interesting alternative for dressing wounds. Unlike conventional wound dressings – which need to be replaced, potentially damaging fragile new tissue – North Atlantic cod skin stays on the wound. The body's cells grow into it, and as new human tissue develops, the cod skin is gradually absorbed and replaced by the patient's own living tissue. Humans have used animal skin to cover wounds since as far back as the 16th century. Pigs became the dominant donor in modern medicine, largely for their affordability as well as their similarity to human skin. But while mammal skin needs to undergo harsh treatment to eliminate the risk of disease transmission, cod skin may carry little risk of spreading disease to humans, since certain pathogens adapted to cold-water fish struggle to survive in the warmer human body, Sigurjónsson explained to us. title: Mind the tone
content: People are notoriously bad at picking up spoken words when caught off-guard, especially in a noisy, crowded train. Passengers with visual impairments need special attention too. A few musical notes work like a familiar tap on the shoulder, prompting our brains to listen. Designing these little jingles is a delicate exercise: the melody needs to cut through the hum of engines and screech of wheels without startling commuters. The jingles must rely on moderately fast “attacks” (that regulate how quickly a sound reaches full volume), sustained “pulse rates” (the speed and spacing between notes), and a range of musical patterns, sometimes ascending, some descending, and others using a back-and-forth sequence. content: “If Europe were to prepare for the Second World War with today's tenders and procedures, then D-Day would happen not in 1944 but in 1951,” Leo Litra, senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told us, referencing research from his ECFR colleagues. The point he is making is one that European leaders have come to see as the crux of our defence. In WWII, the United States and Britain went from serious mobilisation in 1941 to the largest amphibious invasion in history in June 1944, taking roughly two to three years of preparation. title: Sweden (barely) beats the far-right
content: What happened: The Social Democrat-led centre-left opposition very narrowly won parliamentary elections in Sweden, defeating the ruling right-wing minority government, which was supported by the far-right Sweden Democrats. There is a three seat difference between the two blocs. It was so close that counting continued until Wednesday – with a margin of around 27,000 votes. Why this matters: Besides giving Europe's battered centre-left – after a string of electoral losses across the continent – a much-needed victory, the result also offers Europe a lesson: there appears to be a limit to how far voters are willing to accept increasingly restrictive migration policy. title: From Finland to Portugal by train in just 125 hours
content: Last week, Jon Worth, a railway activist who advocates for better cross-border train travel across Europe, completed the longest train journey in the EU – from Kemijärvi in northern Finland to Lagos in southern Portugal – in a speedy 125 hours and 31 minutes. These two locations are about as far apart as you can travel by train within the EU. Worth covered 6,203 km with an Interrail pass, taking 23 trains run by 10 different railway companies. The journey was only possible thanks to the reopening of a railway line between Haparanda in Sweden and Tornio in Finland in August, which had been closed for 38 years. title: Why is Britain going crazy over a medieval embroidery?
content: The Bayeux Tapestry has been on display at the British Museum since 10 September, and everyone in Britain wants to see it. In July, 80,000 people joined the online queue at its peak – some waiting up to nine hours – to get tickets. title: Diplomas of Europe, unite
content: What happened: Yesterday (15 September), the European Commission promised to cut some of the annoying paperwork that makes it harder for EU workers to move to another country. Its proposed Fair Labour Mobility rules aim to make it far quicker to get a diploma recognised in another EU country. Doctors, nurses, engineers – and soon other in-demanded professions such as physiotherapists – could get their diplomas recognised in five weeks instead of three months. Other qualifications would have an 11-week deadline, instead of four months. Social security and health insurance documents, as well as diplomas, would also be available via European digital identity wallets, free mobile apps that store verified personal identification documents. Member states are required to make them a reality across the EU by the end of this year. title: Human rights, but optional
content: On 13 September, Turkish police cracked down on people, bars, and rights groups associated with the LGBTQ+ community. Under the guise of protecting family values, they arrested dozens, including 50 activists from the rights group Kaos GL alone. Kaos GL previously won a legal case at the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) against the Turkish government for another crackdown in 2017. The ECtHR was created to protect the fundamental human rights set out in the European Convention on Human Rights, a post-World War II treaty with 46 European members. It's overseen by the Council of Europe, a separate institution from the EU. When the ECtHR finds that a violation has occurred, its judgment is legally binding, meaning the country is required to comply with it. Yet almost a decade after the judgment in favour of Kaos GL, the Turkish government's attack against LGBTQ+ people has only intensified. title: If you're reading this, you're in the minority
content: In the winter of 2015, Canadian rapper Drake released a mixtape with the plainest cover I'd ever seen: seven words hand-lettered in black on plain white: If You're Reading This It's Too Late. That same year, a non-profit called OpenAI was founded in San Francisco. Nobody linked the two moments. Why would they? Well, seven years later, OpenAI released ChatGPT, and the web hasn't been the same since. AI flooded the space we had spent decades building for each other, one post, one blog, and one comment at a time. The numbers are clear. Stack Overflow was once the beating, chaotic heart of programmer culture, where strangers helped strangers debug their code at 2am. Its monthly questions have collapsed from 109,152 in November 2022, the month ChatGPT launched, to 1,146 in August 2026. title: Couldn't think straight this summer? Same
content: You wake up on a hot morning. You're sweating, and you haven't slept well. Your head aches, the workday ahead makes you anxious, and the birds chirping outside make you want to scream. If you lived through this summer's heatwaves in Europe, you know this is hardly an exaggeration of what a typical day can feel like. Record temperatures had Europeans feeling frustrated and dizzy. Part of the reason has to do with how our brain works. Our brain makes up only 2% of our body mass, but eats up 20% of our energy. During a heatwave or short exposure to extremely high temperatures, the heart struggles to keep everything cool. “The heart has to pump blood to the periphery of the body to help the body sweat, and for that it has to work hard. When heat exceeds our capacity to sweat, the supply of blood to the brain might not be optimal anymore, and the brain starts to overheat,” said Pieter Vancamp, a neurobiologist at the PhanLab in Nantes, France. You might not notice the difference between 30°C and 31°C, but your brain does: even a shift of less than a degree alters our nervous system. title: Eating our way through the city, for free
content: Growing up, I used to walk around the allotments – those small city gardens – to see if any vegetables or fruit hanging over the fence could be put into my belly. I revisited that habit recently, snacking on yellow plums that had begun transforming into jam on the pavement (I went for the ones still round but perfectly ripe). Some gardeners volunteer their harvest, putting apples in boxes on the streets with a little sign saying to “take some”. Urban foraging is hardly new, although collaborative maps and edible-city projects have made it far more visible. Falling Fruit is one such map. Launched in 2013, it shows where there's food up for grabs in cities across the globe. I looked up the closest edible location to me in Brussels on the map – it was a Carrefour dumpster, with a little comment in French: “Some Monday or Thursday evenings, a black container containing bread and sometimes other items.” Alright, how about something offering a more classic foraging experience? There – a pear tree, 37 minutes away on foot. title: Autumn foliage
content: Summer is over and autumn is upon us! While Europe may not have the spectacular autumn landscapes of North America, it offers a smaller but more varied seasonal display. The timing of autumn senescence – the changing colour and falling of leaves – varies widely across the continent. In southern Europe, colours can appear as early as late August, while in central and northern Europe, trees often stay green well into October or even November before changing and shedding their leaves. This visualisation was first published in September 2025.

title: Too hot to holiday
content: While some sunshine fanatics embraced this summer's record-breaking temperatures and booked their beach getaway come what may, an increasing number of tourists travelled to cooler destinations instead. Northern European countries found themselves in the perfect position to offer such a “coolcation”. The number of passengers who booked flights from mainland Europe to Scandinavia in July and August increased by 35% compared to the same period last year, according to data Scandinavian Airlines (SAS) shared with us. Denmark saw the sharpest increase (+60%), followed by Norway (+25%) and Sweden (+20%). “We’re seeing growing interest in Sweden, Norway and Denmark, driven by a desire for nature, open spaces, a slower pace of life and more authentic experiences,” Alexandra Lindgren Kaoukji, head of communications at SAS, told us. “It’s a trend we’ve seen building over several years, and one that is now clearly reflected in our bookings.” Why? title: Are we at war? Are we not at war? We're at hybrid war!
content: On 1 September, the German government did what it had never done before. It blamed Russia for an attempted attack on its soil: an explosive-laden drone placed near a Ukrainian cargo plane at the Leipzig/Halle airport. Had the attack been successful, it could have caused mass casualties. What did Germany do in response? It closed Russia's cultural centre in Berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn. Russia's ambassador got a talking to, with most EU governments joining in. And that was it. Now, you might wonder: is closing a consulate really the most appropriate response to an attempt to blow up an airplane? No, it isn't, and experts are warning that this kind of reaction is inviting Russia to escalate its campaign even further. This year alone, a Russian drone hit a Romanian residential block, injuring two; Russians also set fire to train infrastructure in Latvia while pretending to be Ukrainians; and Russia is constantly jamming GPS over the Baltics, leading to around 123,000 flights disrupted in the first four months of 2025 alone. title: Deportations so shady we had to invent one
content: Back in June, the European Parliament briefly felt like a Trump rally. As the Parliament passed the Return Regulation, set to increase deportations of “illegal” third-country nationals, right-wing parliamentarians chanted “send them back!” Among the reasons for the Return Regulation's popularity is one statistic: of all the non-EU citizens ordered to leave the EU in 2025 (491,950), only around 28% did so. The regulation promises to increase that share by accelerating deportations and allowing member states to negotiate “return hubs” with third countries: centres that can receive “illegal” immigrants. These aren't just attractive options for EU countries looking to remove migrants, but also good deals for third countries, which can expect financial investments in return. In very un-EU fashion, the regulation was fast-tracked, specifically the parts that concern return hubs. Now that the EU has laid out the framework, it’s up to member states to seek out their own agreements. Last Friday (4 September), they did just that. title: The European Waste Awards
content: Europeans throw a lot of stuff away. We're a messy union of, occasionally, trashy people. A feat to celebrate with an extremely serious award ceremony. Granted, the Municipal Waste Reporting Obligation is not the most glamorous duty put forth by the European Union. But after sinking knee-deep into the municipal waste data (which excludes things like industrial and agricultural waste), I was surprised by how much countries' waste profiles differed. Some throw away more clothes, others more food. And call me crazy, but I believe that makes us unique. Tracking what we throw away maps our impact on the planet, but it also shows us what we're up to when nobody's looking. So let's pull back the curtains and shine a spotlight into the deepest and darkest recesses of our trash bins. Welcome to the first-ever European Waste Awards, the smelliest award ceremony of all!

title: What your wine knows about climate change
content: For winemakers across Europe, this year's grape harvest began notably early. In Champagne, France, where grape-picking has historically never started before late August, grapes were already being cut on 12 August. That marks a big shift from the 20th century average start date of 26 September, which held steady until the late 1980s. Champagne is not the only wine region to set a record this year, as a warm spring accelerated the grapes' growth across Europe. Producers of Franciacorta sparkling wine from the Lombardy region in northern Italy even started their harvest in July. “An extraordinary event,” the Franciacorta consortium of winemakers called it. Grape harvests as a climate archive Wine harvests all over Europe have been starting progressively earlier, which according to climate historian Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie is a good indicator of climate change. He was among the first to use historical records to study past climates. Just like the timing of ice-breaking in northern European ports or cherry blossom seasons in Japan, the start of the grape harvest is shaped both by nature's rythm and human decisions. title: Affordable housing without the housing
content: The European Commission unveiled an Affordable Housing Act this week that promises more than it can deliver. Dan Jørgensen, the EU's commissioner for housing, told reporters that the legislation won't “lead to cheap houses for everybody in Europe”. It will instead help cities to justify action against short-term rentals, second homes, or vacant dwellings. They could do that if an area is found to be under housing stress, meaning house prices and rental costs far outstrip local incomes. Short-term rentals have boomed in cities popular with tourists. Listings on big platforms nearly doubled between 2018 and 2024. Central Madrid has around 40 such rentals compared to 100 available on long-term contracts, the Commission said. Cities have been striking back. Barcelona will ban short-term rentals from 2028. Amsterdam and Vienna have already restricted them in certain areas. Paris has capped how many nights homes can be rented out for. Right now, these cities risk costly legal challenges, even if they've won cases against short-term rentals in court. title: We're still farming fur for what?
content: Europe has been turning its back on fur for a while now. As consumer demand has fallen, the fur industry has shrunk sharply over the past decade. The number of fur farms in the EU has fallen by 73%, pelt production by 86%, sales by 92%, and employment by 86–92%, according to a 2025 report by animal welfare organisations. Fur is an unprofitable industry that costs Europeans more than it generates in economic value. It reduces the EU economy, generating a loss of €9.2 million in gross value added per year and around €446 million in environmental and health costs. So why is the EU still importing fur, from Russia of all places? In April, the EU banned imports of tanned furskins from Russia as part of a sanctions package. In July, just three months later, EU governments allowed an exemption for Russian sable pelt imports. “Apparently, it’s very difficult to get them anywhere else,” a senior EU official told Euractiv. title: Big corporate fish eat little boats
content: After a life at sea, José Correia doesn't want his son to follow the same path – the work as a fisher is physically challenging and the income unattractive. José's community in Angeiras, a village on Portugal’s northern coast, is ageing fast. He now counts only “five or six” young fishers. The same is happening around Europe: only one in four artisanal fishers in the EU are under 40. Small boats constitute around 76% of the EU's active fishing fleet and almost half the workforce, according to Seas At Risk, an environmental group. But they land only about 7% of catches by weight. The rest goes into the hands of bigger players. Just five Dutch groups control around 16% of the EU fleet when measured in tonnes. Small-scale fishers are also catching much less than they used to. Between 2018 and 2022, their catch value shrank around 30% in the Mediterranean, 36% in the Baltic, and 50% in the Black Sea, according to a European Commission report. Brian O’Riordan, policy adviser at Low Impact Fishers of Europe (LIFE), says the fishing sector is in a “dire” spot, and “at a crossroads”. title: Teenagers are falling behind, and we aren't catching them
content: Every three years, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) tests how well 15-year-olds can parse a long text, handle mathematical calculations, and solve some scientific problems. Last year, it quizzed its largest group ever: more than 760,000 teenagers born in 2009 and 2010 from 91 countries. This is the generation that learned to walk as smartphones took off. They were born during a global financial crisis and saw their schools closed during the Covid-19 pandemic. The results of last year's OECD PISA test aren't pretty. Students had the lowest average ever recorded for reading and maths. Reading scores fell sharply in the last three years after peaking in 2012. One in five students are low performers, meaning they lack the skills needed to get more education, participate meaningfully in society, and get high-quality and well-paid work. No European country saw its score improve, apart from science performance in the United Kingdom, Slovakia, and Türkiye. title: Justice for pigeons!
content: You'd struggle to find a city or a town on the European continent that pigeons haven't made their home. They've lived alongside people for thousands of years, and were among the first domesticated birds. Today, humanity has abandoned its former friends: pigeons feed on garbage and face deadly threats in cities, from heavy traffic to bird nets and spikes trying to stop them from nesting on buildings. Every day, many suffer injuries as they try to survive in our concrete jungles. Help is hard to find. Because they aren't classified as typical wildlife, nor as pets or farm animals, both private veterinarians and wildlife rescue centres are reluctant to treat them. Světlana Vávrová and Veronika Petráková from Czechia decided to change that, and have been rescuing injured pigeons for years. “I've always felt sympathy for these birds,” Petráková told us. “The situations we've seen in the streets motivated us to act.” This year, the project is growing. title: Building a riviera
content: Yachts, swanky shops, and high-end French restaurants are probably what you associate with the term riviera. So did I, until I learned about the Albanian Riviera. Stretching across the southern coast of Albania, the riviera has helped the country attract millions of tourists in recent years, as it offers a similar experience to its French or Italian counterparts at lower prices. The rise in tourist arrivals to Albania has been meteoric, doubling in just four years. The Trump and Kushner families have infamously also taken a liking to the natural beauty of the region, financing real estate developments in an environmentally protected section of the coastline. The resulting fiasco unleashed massive protests across Albania, and 100 days on, they show no sign of stopping. But Albania isn't the first to adopt the label for itself. The original riviera was just a stretch of coast around Genoa, Italy – in Ligurian, riviera simply means “coastline”. Since then, coastal regions far beyond Italy and France have learned that the word is an effective marketing campaign. title: Who let the pomegranates in?
content: When Belgian botanist Roosmarijn Steeman knelt down to take inventory of plants growing in Brussels, she spotted a pomegranate bush on the pavement. Another day, she was surprised to find a date plant thriving. Her observations are part of the FloraBru project, a four-year effort to catalogue all wild plants Brussels has to offer. “We see many Mediterranean plants doing really well in Brussels,” Steeman told us. The fact these plants can thrive in the city has to do with the heat-island effect: concrete absorbs heat in cities, and only partly releases it during the night. Temperatures are generally higher and winters milder than in the countryside. “Also, Mediterranean plants typically like stone and rocky environments, which means they thrive in cities,” Steeman added. Take the (scarily named) “baby’s tears”, a plant native to Sardinia and Corsica which nowadays finds it warm enough in cities like Brussels, Ghent, Antwerp, and Belgium's milder coastal area. Another successful migrant is small goosegrass, native to northern Africa, south-west Asia, and southern Europe, but now spotted in urban centres in Belgium, the UK, Germany, and Czechia. title: Europe promised to ban cages, but industry got the biggest say
content: Each year, more than 300 million farm animals in the EU live in cages. Europeans overwhelmingly want that to change: 84% think the welfare of farmed animals should be improved, and 60% are even willing to pay more for it, according to a 2023 Eurobarometer survey. The European Food Safety Authority also recommends avoiding the use of cages for broiler chickens and laying hens to improve animal health and welfare. In 2021, the European Commission committed to ending caged farming following the European Citizens’ Initiative (ECI) “End the Cage Age”, which gathered more than 1.4 million signatures and support from over 170 organisations for a complete ban on cages for farmed animals. The European Parliament voted in favour of the initiative with overwhelming support, and the Commission promised to propose legislation by the end of 2023 to “phase out, and finally prohibit, the use of cage systems” for the animals mentioned in the initiative: hens, rabbits, quail, ducks, geese, pigs, and calves. title: The reaper came early this year
content: Winter wheat reached harvest stage earlier than usual in most EU regions this year, according to our analysis of European Commission crop forecasting data. A very clear sign that late summer arrived ahead of schedule. France stood out: on average, wheat maturity came around 15 days earlier than long-term average. In much of central Europe, the difference was about a week to ten days. Repeated heatwaves sped up the winter crops and shortened grain filling, the period during which wheat kernels gain much of their weight, according to the European Commission JRC MARS Bulletin report. This brought the harvest forward across western and central Europe. So what happens when the reaper comes early? When heat and drought force ripening, the grain ends up smaller and yields fall, because kernels have less time and water to put on weight. In Hauts-de-France, France's leading wheat-producing region, an Argus media survey indicated yields were about 7% lower than the ten-year regional average. title: Why the heat is killing more women than men
content: “Those who die during a heatwave do so for social, rather than meteorological reasons.” This is one of the sobering conclusions in a recent report by IDRA, a Barcelona-based urban research institute. The report identifies a recurring profile among heat-related deaths: elderly, sick women from low-income neighbourhoods without access to air conditioning. There were 56% more heat-related deaths in women than in men during the summer of 2022, once life expectancy had been factored in, according to this analysis. Still, only looking at death tolls is “myopic”, or short-sighted, according to Ronita Bardhan, environment and health professor at Cambridge University. There are no significant physiological differences in how both sexes cope with heat. Instead, social factors can make women more vulnerable to its effects, Bardhan told The European Correspondent. Everything starts with where you live. Living in an uninsulated flat in a densely populated area means heat accumulates inside the home during a heatwave, even if it has air conditioning. “If your building cannot flush out the heat trapped during the day, you are practically inside an oven,” Bardhan said. title: Bulgaria knows how to store the sun
content: When it comes to leadership in clean technologies and renewable energy, you'd probably first think of countries like Sweden or the Netherlands. But today, we're heading southeast. Around 35% of Bulgaria's electricity comes from fossil fuels, so it may not seem like a leader in the green energy transition. But Bulgaria has one surprising strength: batteries for renewable energy. Bulgaria went from virtually zero battery storage in 2023 to a current capacity of 14 gigawatt-hours (GWh), transforming the country not only into a regional, but also a global leader in the sector – for comparison, the EU as a whole has 77.3 GWh battery capacity. Such large storage allows Bulgaria to save its renewable electricity (mostly solar) for later use when the sun stops shining. It also helps with balancing out the grid, which can get overwhelmed during peak production hours. Storing its excess electricity has allowed Bulgaria to keep power prices down, even during the periods when they normally climb – like for example when you come back home after your workday. title: Far-right extremist party gets 43.8% in German state
content: What happened: In closely watched regional elections in the east German state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won 43.8% of the vote. It may form a government there, the first time since 1945 that a right-wing extremist party did so in Germany. Why this matters: It is the party's best result yet in any state, and another step in its steady rise. Saxony-Anhalt is far from the only place where it dominates: Nationally, the AfD has topped the polls for several months, with support hovering around 30%. Germany's domestic intelligence agency has formally classified the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch as “far-right extremist”. Among the reasons cited are the pursuit of an ethnically homogeneous society. The AfD wants to leave the euro, deport millions of people, including naturalised German citizens, and restart trade relations with Russia. title: Your online pharmacy is probably not a pharmacy
content: In a global operation earlier this year, Interpol dismantled 66 criminal groups and seized over 6 million doses of unapproved and counterfeit pharmaceuticals. The groups were trafficking products such as sedatives or antibiotics, often by mislabelling them as health supplements or “cancer treatment kits” to escape regulations. Both worldwide and in Europe, the illicit medicine market is growing. This year, Europol dismantled a large network producing and shipping fake products, spanning Bulgaria, Greece, Moldova, Romania, Hungary, and Poland. Fake pharmacies draw consumers in by offering low prices. title: From a job offer in Russia to a Ukrainian prison cell
content: Jean Unana signed a piece of paper he couldn't read. Weeks later, he was hiding among corpses in a forest, eating from the rations of dead men to survive. He is not a soldier. title: A quaking continent
content: Since June, Europe has been hit by more than 11,000 earthquakes, according to data from the European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre. This number is not unusual for a continent sitting on tectonic ridges and fault lines. However, just 13% had a magnitude above 2.5, which is generally the threshold detectable by humans. Only a single earthquake had a magnitude above 6: it struck on 2 June off the coast of Calabria, sending light tremors across most of Sicily and southern mainland Italy. Large parts of the Mediterranean, the Balkans, and Türkiye are earthquake hotspots. An estimated 35% of Europeans live within a moderate or high seismic hazard zone. Despite most earthquakes being harmless, experts from the World Bank Group and the Global Facility for Disaster Reduction and Recovery warn that Europe is not sufficiently equipped to handle this kind of natural hazard. A combination of low public awareness, an ageing housing stock, and vulnerable critical services leaves Europeans exposed to both earthquakes and secondary hazards such as landslides and tsunamis.

title: How can we actually beat the heat?
content: Extreme heat has killed over 200,000 Europeans in the past four years, and this year’s heatwaves added at least 35,000 more deaths. What’s actually being done to beat it? The good news: heat prevention plans like early warning systems, cooling shelters, and check-in systems are effective: a 2025 study across 14 European countries over nearly 30 years found that prevention plans cut heat-related mortality by 25%. Antonio Gasparrini, one of the study's authors and an epidemiologist at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, told us he was struck by how clear the result was: “There is a very strong signal of effects of such interventions. It was strong evidence.” So what works? While we know heat prevention plans work, we don't know which interventions work best. Gasparrini said “there wasn't strong evidence of difference in interventions,” partly because plans vary too much by country to compare. France is a European leader in heat mortality prevention. After a catastrophic heatwave claimed almost 15,000 lives in 2003, the country established one of the world’s first comprehensive response frameworks. title: A sky full of... satellites
content: Maybe you've seen them, or pictures of them: a neat line of “stars” travelling through the night sky. What they were seeing was Elon Musk's Starlink satellites, lit by a Sun that had already set on Earth. The brightest satellites don't need a telescope to be spotted – on some nights, you can see them with your own eyes. title: Europe’s internal migrants
content: Imagine a young Romanian guy, let's call him Mihai, let's say he's 25 years old. After finishing his vocational training and trying out a couple of jobs, his employment prospects in Romania don't look very promising, so he starts looking for opportunities abroad. A few weeks later, he moves to Bavaria and starts work in a construction company, where the pay is significantly higher than in Romania. This profile is fictional, but could well be real. title: Violence is a male problem
content: Over a week ago, an 18-year-old man killed a 17-year-old girl with a sword in a Swedish school, heavily injuring two others. Police found an account, linked to him, sharing previous mass killers' videos. A few days later, a 16-year-old boy who had encouraged him over encrypted messages was also arrested. That's just the most recent example: from petty crime to rape and terrifying extremist attacks, the overwhelming majority of crime is committed by men. In 2024, only 1 in 18 adult prisoners in the EU were women. This figure is very similar be it in Finland or Romania, in countries with high or low migration, or in countries with high or low crime rates. We looked in detail at crime rates in Sweden and the three largest European countries, and they speak for themselves: Most perpetrators are young men. According to UN data from 2023, roughly 44% of homicide suspects worldwide were aged 15-29. Men of that age are also the group at highest risk of being killed globally. While homicides have decreased by 11% in the last decade, rape and sexual violence increased by 7% and 10% respectively in the same period, likely linked to increased awareness. title: When is it too hot to work?
content: In July 2022, José Antonio González, a 60 year old street cleaner in Madrid, collapsed from heatstroke while working outdoors in the heat. When the emergency services arrived, his body temperature was over 41ºC. After his death, his family found searches on his computer for the symptoms of heatstroke and how to prevent it. One year later Spain passed a law to protect those who work outdoors during heatwaves, ensuring employers adapt or reduce working times when the national weather service issues an orange or red heat alert. Across Europe 130 million workers are exposed to dangerous heat on the job, with 230 deaths and 277,000 injuries at work each year. There is currently no EU-wide law setting a maximum temperature for outdoor work. Right now this is left to each individual country to decide. In Belgium, temperature is assessed using the wet bulb scale, which also takes into account humidity and wind. In Portugal, indoor workplaces must keep temperatures between 18 and 25ºC. Germany sets no binding limit at all, only voluntary guidelines that employers can ignore. In Greece, the Acropolis has seen several shutdowns at midday, sparing staff and visitors the hottest hours. title: Are fake meats bad for you?
content: Plant-based meats are on the rise – and there is plenty of talk about their supposed nutritional up- and downsides. Critics argue they contain too much salt, too little protein, and that they taste like... well, you get the gist. A 2025 study published in Frontiers in Nutrition compared real and fake meats in Germany, Romania, and Ireland, offering a European answer to the question whether these culinary innovations are good news for your health. While contents differ across products and markets – the average plant-based burger doesn't exist – plant-based meats generally contain less saturated fats and more fibre than their meat counterparts. Protein remains higher in real meats, while salt levels are similar. So, does that mean they're healthier? As you've probably heard before, nutrition is a game of balance and variety: the goal is not to eat too much, or too little, of anything. That said, four grams of extra fibre doesn't hurt; fewer saturated fats are probably good for you, too. content: Make the most polluting companies pay for their CO2 emissions and use the revenues to pay for new green buses in Hungary or flood risk management in Estonia. title: Who's really angry
content: Young Europeans are a highly visible presence on the streets, with Gen Z among the age groups most likely to participate in demonstrations. They're increasingly locked out of affordable housing across the continent, and many report intense climate anxiety. During Covid-19, mental health data showed particularly low wellbeing among young Europeans compared with older groups. All in all, Gen Z would appear to be anxious, angry, and struggling. Except when you ask them directly. 48% of 15- to 24-year-olds say they feel hopeful and 40% feel confident. Of all age groups, they reported the highest rates of every positive emotion, according to data from the Eurobarometer. The pattern is reversed when it comes to negative emotions. Only 6% of young Europeans said they felt angry. That figure triples to 18% among 40- to 54-year-olds. Helplessness sits at 15% among the youngest group and rises to 27% among those 55 and over. So yes, there is indeed a troubled generation in Europe right now. It just may not be the one everyone keeps talking about.

title: Europe's €800 billion gamble
content: The EU will be shutting down “the largest stimulus package ever financed” at the end of this year. The €800 billion NextGenerationEU programme was meant to be a massive and much-needed public investment boost to make Europe “greener, more digital, and more resilient”. It paid for Florence's new tramway expansion. It paid for Spain to expand electric car charging networks. It paid to connect the Greek island of Santorini and other islands to the Greece's mainland power grid. But the recovery fund is also riddled with flaws. Narrow rules about what the money can pay for mean EU governments have been slow to spend the full package of loans and grants, which as a result has shrunk to about €575 billion. Governments, already burdened by debt, have been particularly reluctant to take loans from the fund, leaving €95 billion unclaimed. Three EU countries – Italy, Spain, and Greece – have soaked up a disproportionate amount of the funding. title: Iceland keeps the door to the EU shut
content: What happened: Icelandic citizens voted against resuming EU accession talks on Saturday, keeping Iceland’s long-running EU membership bid closed. 52.8% of Icelanders said “no” to reopening talks, with a strong urban/rural split. Formally joining the EU would have however required a second referendum. Turnout was reported to have been at 82.5%, the highest in any Icelandic election since 2009. Iceland’s fishing industry was at the forefront of public debate, as Iceland’s fisheries make up 40% of its goods exports, which Iceland's public feared would become subject to EU control. Why this matters: It comes as a blow to the EU's already challenging enlargement agenda as Iceland would have been a strong showcase for its enlargement policy. Iceland is a stable, wealthy country, and is already a member of the European Economic Area, as well as the Schengen border-free zone. The vote also came amid diminishing trust in the US as a security partner, alongside US president Trump’s push to acquire Greenland, Iceland’s closest neighbour (often confusing the two). title: Europe's rivers are warning us with our ancestor's handwriting
content: Europe’s major rivers are at record low water levels: the Rhine and the Danube, the Po in Italy, and the Loire in France. Across central Europe, retreating water has exposed hunger stones used as warning markers between the 15th and 19th centuries when rivers' water levels were exceptionally low. These warnings meant the drought would likely lead to crop failures and famine. The most famous one, which hasn't resurfaced as of 27 August, lies in the Elbe near Děčín, Czechia, and dates back to 1417. It reads: “Wenn du mich siehst, dann weine” – German for “If you see me, weep.” Low water levels have also exposed World War II artefacts and mammoth bones: a Wehrmacht motorcycle in Budapest, Nazi-era warships in the Serbian stretch of the Danube, and the remains of mammoth in Ryahovo, Bulgaria. In France and Romania, nuclear power plants had to be shut down as the Danube’s water could no longer cool them. Many goods are transported over those rivers, as doing so is both cheaper and greener than sending them by road. title: Europe's burning peat is taking centuries of carbon with it
content: From the end of July to mid-August, drought-fuelled wildfires tore through two of Europe's valuable peatlands, the Belgian High Fens (Hautes Fagnes) and England's Great Fen. Within days, despite the inexhaustible efforts of fire crews, parts of the once-lush wetlands were reduced to barren, moon-like landscapes. It's a stark warning for an increasingly dehydrated continent. Both Fens are composed of centuries of dead vegetation compressed by water into peat, creating wetlands acting as dense carbon stores that store twice as much carbon as all forests on the planet. But that carbon-storing capacity is reliant on water. Dried out by plantation and agriculture and now stressed by drought and heat, the Fens have proven catastrophically incendiary. Peat fires are notoriously hard to control because they burn downward, below the ground's surface and out of reach, and can keep smouldering for weeks or months. “Some of the fires out here are one or two metres deep now,” Lorna Parker, project manager at the Great Fen nature restoration project, told The European Correspondent. “And obviously that's a massive release of carbon into the atmosphere. content: In German politics, all eyes are on the state of Saxony-Anhalt where a state election on 6 September could prove a pivotal moment. title: Is it a bribe? Blackmail? Or the future of European defence?
content: In 1985, the UK struck its biggest-ever export agreement, selling weapons and fighter jets worth £40 billion to Saudi-Arabia. As part of this deal, the British firm BAE Systems would channel investment and joint ventures back to Saudi-Arabia, including £1 billion to Saudi's prince Bandar bin Sultan himself. This kind of arrangement is known as a defence offset: money a foreign military supplier promises to invest in the buyer's economy as a condition of the sale. Imagine buying a car and having the dealer throw in a free trailer or even something with nothing to do with the car at all, like offering to pay off part of your mortgage. Europe is the world's largest receiver of defence offsets, receiving an estimated €160 billion of the €340 billion total paid in offsets worldwide between 2021 and 2025. Though not very visible, these offset deals may represent as much as half of all global defence trade, according to offsets expert Ron Matthews. title: The Belgian parenting hack: abandoning children in the woods
content: Every summer on a dark evening, Belgian children as young as 11 are dropped off somewhere they don't know and told to find their way to a campsite. Without an adult or a smartphone. title: Vuelta around Europe
content: In the world of road cycling, much revolves around three big races: the Tour de France, Giro d'Italia, and Vuelta a España. Together they form the Grand Tours – the most prestigious events on the road bike calendar every year. In recent years, they've grown more international. Every few years, part of a race – usually its ceremonial start, along with some of the days that follow – now unfolds in a neighbouring or nearby country. But until now, no single city had ever hosted the opening of all three. Having welcomed both the Tour and the Giro before, Monaco added the Vuelta this past weekend, completing the set. A handful of other cities, while never hosting the start of a tour, have staged the beginning or end of individual stages across all three tours, most notably Utrecht in the Netherlands and Turin in Italy. content: This Saturday, Icelanders will vote in a referendum on whether or not to reopen membership negotiations with the EU. Iceland and the EU have had a long-standing situationship. title: Power plants struggle in the heat, Ukraine has a solution
content: This summer's heatwaves have put our energy infrastructure to the test. From overheating nuclear reactors to wind turbines standing still in wind droughts, extreme heat is an energy challenge we can't afford to take lightly. Low water levels in rivers are the main problem, since they affect most power plants. Whether gas-powered, coal-fired, or nuclear; all rely on rivers' levels being high enough to feed their cooling systems. There are also limits for how much hot water used for cooling can be sent back into the rivers without killing fish and causing harm to the local environment. During extreme heat, power plants often have to reduce their energy output to comply with these regulations. title: Even the oceans are struggling to keep their cool
content: On Saturday, 22 August, global ocean surface temperatures hit the highest ever recorded. In Europe, mid-August these temperatures reached around 6°C above average in the western Mediterranean Sea and above 5°C in the Atlantic off the Iberian Peninsula, according to Copernicus Marine Service data. Marine heatwaves across Europe have grown more widespread over the past decades. The share of our waters experiencing marine heatwaves has increased from 40% in the 1980s to 98% in 2025. The current situation is “very serious”, according to Zoe Jacobs, a senior researcher at the National Oceanography Centre in the United Kingdom. Jacobs is an expert in marine heatwaves in the UK and surrounding North Atlantic. “We are experiencing the longest and most intense marine heatwave that we have ever had,” she said. The past few years have seen a sharp rise in the most intense heatwaves, with sea temperatures far above the normal range for a given location and season. title: Germans love getting naked
content: Summer isn't over yet. In Germany, a common way to spend it is by the lakes or the Baltic Sea. For many non-Germans, though, it comes as a bit of a culture shock: there are naked people walking around, and nobody seems to care. Germany is one of the most relaxed countries in the world when it comes to public nudity. Parks, beaches, and campsites often set aside dedicated spaces for naturists, and there's a high tolerance for mixing between the dressed and the undressed. Germany's “free body culture” (Freikörperkultur or FKK) roots can be traced back to the late 19th century, when (mostly) white-collar men in Protestant, urban Germany sought a return to nature as a response to rising industrialisation. “The idea was to expose the whole body to sun, air, water, and other natural elements to contribute to its well-being. It also included exercising,” explains Maren Möhring, a cultural historian and nudism expert at Leipzig University. By the early 20th century, it became a mass movement, with hundreds of FKK clubs with their own grounds where members could be nude together, as well as dedicated public spaces where people are allowed to be naked. title: Europe's silent heat death toll
content: It’s not news that it’s hot: this summer, we’ve had five major heatwaves. Extreme heat killed at least 25,000 people in Western Europe alone, according to a Bloomberg analysis. In Wallonia, Belgium, more deaths were recorded on June 28, the peak of June’s heatwave, than any given day at the height of the Covid-19 pandemic. Belgium was the country hardest hit during the month of June, together with France and Germany, according to data collected by the European Mortality Monitoring Network. Some 80 million people across the continent faced temperatures of 40ºC and higher, often in places unadapted to such temperatures. Yet heat mortality is nothing new. Over the past four years, extreme heat has killed more than 200,000 Europeans. Nearly all of those deaths were preventable, Europe’s regional director for the World Health Organization, Hans Kluge, stated in a speech this June. A history of heat Our first wake-up call in Europe came in 2003, when more than 70,000 excess deaths were recorded – meaning there were 70,000 more deaths than would normally be expected during that period. title: Europe's (not so) border-free zone
content: “Currently stuck in a huge traffic jam on my way back to Hendaye (France) from Irun (Spain),” messaged Gosia Szczodrowska, who answered my call for people who'd faced a Schengen border check they didn't expect this month. Gosia was on holiday in southern France and had made a short trip across the border to Spain. But on her way back, French police were checking all vehicles, “which makes this let’s-go-have-ice-cream-in-Spain trip an entire afternoon of travelling.” Both France and Spain are part of Europe's Schengen area. There usually aren't any border checks when travelling between two Schengen countries. 3.5 million people make trips across Schengen borders every day, often because the nearest school or supermarket to their home is in another country. The Schengen zone counts 29 European countries, 25 of them in the EU plus Norway, Switzerland, Iceland, and Liechtenstein. It has 450 million residents across more than 4.5 million square kilometres. Getting rid of border controls 21 years ago was intended to knit these areas closer together and encourage more Europeans to travel to or work in another EU country. title: When Britain was cool
content: 31 years ago today, the Battle of Britpop reached its climax. One week earlier, on 14 August 1995, Britain's two most popular bands had released a single on the same day: Blur with Country House, and Oasis with Roll With It. The press branded it the Battle of Britpop, and people rushed to music stores to buy whichever copy would prove which band they liked best. Britpop had recently emerged as a reaction against American grunge, the moody, nihilistic sound of bands like Nirvana and Pearl Jam. Where grunge was dark, Britpop was bright and optimistic, built on catchy, guitar-driven pop. It also carried a strong sense of place, a distinctly British aesthetic, and lyrics that captured the reality of everyday life in Britain. Both Blur and Oasis had broken through in 1994. Releasing singles on the same day turned the race to sell the most copies into the perfect story to fill the summer news vacuum. For one week, the Battle of Britpop was national news. On 20 August, the results came in. Blur won the Battle, selling more copies throughout the week. title: Ode to cloudberry
content: When my family brought cloudberries home from the bog, the ripe ones always went straight onto pancakes or into jars; the green ones we spread across a blanket to ripen. I grew up in northern Latvia thinking cloudberries were completely normal. Only much later did I realise how rare they really are (we've made a map for you below). And how they can help us recover degraded wetlands. Cloudberries go by many names, including Arctic berries. They look like plump, amber-orange raspberries, and they taste like heaven: tart, fruity, somewhat floral, with a hint of honey and crunchy seeds to spice it up. In northern Europe, they're common. Cloudberries grow all over Finland and are enjoyed in the form of jam and desserts. The further south you go, however, the map gets patchier. In both Poland and Czechia, they're considered rare glacial relics. Cloudberry plants grow in peatlands and boggy forests and bear fruit under very specific conditions. When they struggle, it's an early indication of changing climate. title: Meet the companies running our borders
content: If you travelled through Europe this summer, you probably noticed pretty long queues: whether in airports in Greece, Italy, Belgium, Germany, or the Netherlands, congestions at border controls often took twice as long as last year. Behind the long queues is the EU's new Entry/Exit System (EES), which replaced passport stamps and introduced face scans and fingerprint collections for non-EU citizens crossing into the EU. Technical faults and staff shortages slowed the roll-out down. While you might've seen the queues, the EU institution and private companies behind the system are less visible. To be honest, we can't blame anyone for not closely following the European Union Agency for the Operational Management of Large-Scale IT Systems in the Area of Freedom, Security and Justice – or eu-LISA, the mother of all EU-acronyms. Despite being a mouthful, you should probably remember the name: Over the past seven years, eu-LISA and partners have gradually built “the most significant expansion of border surveillance in EU history,” Bárbara Simão, programme officer at the human rights group ARTICLE 19, told us. title: You can buy the game, but it's never really yours
content: The iconic action-adventure video game Grand Theft Auto is going all-virtual for its first new edition in 13 years, which is expected to reach €3-5 billion in sales by the end of its first week. Instead of a CD, fans will be buying a printed code in a box. And many of them aren’t happy about it. “What are we actually buying? We are buying a code that gives us access to a game, and we could potentially lose that access if our account is hacked,” João Vale, a 29-year-old teacher living in Valencia and a lifelong gamer, told The European Correspondent. “The company saves money by selling a code instead of producing a disc, but the consumer still pays the same price.” Many of the cultural products we love have gone digital over the past three decades. We pay subscriptions to stream music and movies while second-hand stores fill up with unloved CDs, DVDs, and videotapes. There are huge benefits in being able to take our music with us anywhere we go and being able to pick up new episodes of a must-see show when we’re away from home. title: Why Sweden dominates pop music
content: Sweden regularly punches above its musical weight. ABBA, Denniz Pop, Avicii, Swedish House Mafia, Robyn, and now Zara Larsson dominate global music – quite a lot of stars for a country of just 10 million people. Even more successful are its songwriters. One stands out in particular: Max Martin, who holds the record for the most Billboard Hot 100 number-one songs as producer of 28 hits, and comes second as a songwriter with 30 hits, trailing only Paul McCartney. These include anything from We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together by Taylor Swift and So What by P!nk to I Kissed a Girl by Katy Perry. Martin tops a long list of successful Swedish songwriters. In 2024, the country counted 100,000 songwriters, four times as many as the UK has per capita. title: Plants are flowering earlier because of climate change
content: The world is not the same when temperatures increase – we've felt it with the recent heatwaves. Like us, plants change their “behaviours” with the seasons – and in response to climate change. Scientists have found that so-called “first flowering dates”, or the first day of the year a plant is observed in bloom, are happening earlier. In the most robust study, researchers looked at almost half a million observations spanning 406 plant species between 1753 and 2019. They found that plants in the UK flowered 26 days earlier after 1987 compared to the years before. The pattern holds elsewhere in Europe, with Mediterranean shrubs flowering 20 days earlier over the last 35 years.  Sadly, these dramatic changes are not without consequences. Insects that depend on certain flowers might find they have emerged too late, which is bad news for the birds hoping to eat said insects, and so on. As the world's food web tries to rearrange itself at record speed, plants are being pushed to adapt to an uncertain future.

title: Can Europe keep the data centre boom clean?
content: As I peeked out from the airplane window on my way to Finland, a giant hole in the ground stared back up at me. I thought I was seeing a surface mine, but no: Microsoft is building a giant data centre site close to Helsinki. So far, most data centres in Europe have been built in Western and Central Europe, but the “AI boom” is now driving data centre construction in European countries with cheap, renewable electricity: mostly the Nordics, Spain, and Portugal. Today, the EU has around 3,000 data centres – see our map here. The European Commission aims to triple the EU's data centre capacity by 2035. It's an ambitious goal, but if successful, that tripling would still result in only a fraction of the capacity in the US or China. An even bigger challenge is fitting data centres into our energy system without sacrificing Europe's transition to clean power. The European Commission is currently preparing a sustainability rating scheme for data centres around the bloc, using the same labelling system as we see on our household appliances, from a green A to a red G. title: Heatwaves are roasting millions of farmed animals alive
content: Drink water, stay in the shade, protect your skin – as we live through intense heatwaves this summer, these recommendations are everywhere. The human death toll from the heat is already in the tens of thousands – but what about the billions of farmed animals crammed into sheds, with nowhere to escape the heat? In France, up to 3 million chickens died from heat in just a few days this June. Some farms in Brittany had to count their losses in thousands. “It is a massive psychological shock for farmers,” the representative of the farmers' union FNSEA, Thierry Houel, told the local public radio ICI Bretagne. In some regions of France, so many animals died that carcass collection and disposal processes couldn't keep up, so farmers were exceptionally allowed to bury their dead animals on farms. Still, burials must be carried out under inspection by hydrogeologists to avoid water contamination. Although on an exceptional scale this year, the problem of animal deaths due to heat is far from new.
